# Applications

A BurgerAPI app is an instance of the `Burger` class. Create it in `src/index.ts` and start it with `serve`.

```ts title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const burger = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
});

burger.serve(4000);
```

## Where things live

Each concern has its own file:

| Concern | Where |
|---------|-------|
| Runtime options | `new Burger({...})` in `src/index.ts` |
| Routes | `src/api/**/route.ts`. See [Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/routing) |
| Global hooks | `src/hooks.ts`. See [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system) |
| Plugins | `src/plugins.ts`. See [Hooks and Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins) |
| Shared services | `src/providers.ts`. See [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers) |
| OpenAPI metadata | `src/openapi.config.ts`. See [OpenAPI & Swagger](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/openapi) |
| Build settings | `burger.build.ts` (CLI only) |

All files except `src/index.ts` are optional. For the options of `new Burger`, see [Server Options](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/server-options).

## Related

- [Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/routing)
- [Handlers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/handlers)
- [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration)
- [Burger Class](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/burger-class)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/routing'
---

# Routing

BurgerAPI uses file-based routing. The folders and files under your API directory become HTTP routes. You do not register routes by hand.

- `products/route.ts` becomes `/api/products`.
- A folder named `[id]` captures one segment into `ctx.params.id`.
- A folder named `[...]` captures the rest of the path into `ctx.wildcardParams`.
- A folder named `(group)` organizes files and does not appear in the URL.

When several routes match, the most specific wins: static, then `[param]`, then `[...]`.

See [File-Based Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing) for the full guide.

## Related

- [Applications](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/applications)
- [Handlers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/handlers)
- [Request Context](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/request-handling)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/handlers'
---

# Handlers

A route file exports one function per HTTP method: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`. Each handler gets `ctx` and returns a standard `Response`.

```ts title="src/api/products/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ items: [] });
}

export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const body = await ctx.json();
  return Response.json({ created: true }, { status: 201 });
}
```

`HEAD` and `OPTIONS` are handled for you.

## Reading the request

Use `ctx.params`, `ctx.query`, `ctx.cookies` and `ctx.json()`. See [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api) for the full list.

## Typed, validated data

Put schemas in `schema.ts` and wrap the handler with `defineRoute`. `ctx.validated` is then typed for you.

```ts title="src/api/products/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = { query: z.object({ limit: z.coerce.number().optional() }) };
```

```ts title="src/api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { limit } = ctx.validated.query;
  return Response.json({ limit });
});
```

See [Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/validation).

## Related

- [Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/routing)
- [Request Context](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/request-handling)
- [Response Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/response-types)
- [Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/validation)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core/request-handling'
---

# Request Context

Every handler and hook gets `ctx`, a `BurgerContext`. It holds everything about the current request.

```ts title="src/api/users/[id]/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const { id } = ctx.params;
  return Response.json({ id });
}
```

What you get on `ctx`:

- `ctx.params` and `ctx.wildcardParams`: path parameters.
- `ctx.query`: the query string.
- `ctx.cookies`: cookies.
- `ctx.headers`, `ctx.method`, `ctx.url`, `ctx.json()`, `ctx.text()`: the usual request fields.
- `ctx.request`: the original `Request`.
- `ctx.validated`: data that passed your schemas.
- `ctx.route`: the matched route.
- `ctx.config`: the route's `config.ts` values.
- `ctx.services`: services from `src/providers.ts`.
- `ctx.set`: status, headers and cookies for the response.

`ctx` is not a `Request`. Use `ctx.request` when you need the raw object.

See [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api) for examples of each field.

## Typed validated data

Wrap the handler with `defineRoute` to type `ctx.validated` from the route's `schema.ts`:

```ts title="src/api/users/[id]/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { id } = ctx.validated.params; // typed from the schema
  return Response.json({ id });
});
```

See [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety).

## Related

- [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api)
- [Handlers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/handlers)
- [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation)
- [Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/routing)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/hooks'
---

# Hooks

Hooks run your code at fixed points of a request. There are six: `onRequest`, `transform`, `beforeRoute`, `afterRoute`, `mapResponse` and `onError`.

```
onRequest -> Routing -> transform -> Validation -> beforeRoute
  -> Handler -> afterRoute -> mapResponse
```

Errors go to `onError`.

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import type { GlobalHooks } from "burger-api";

export const beforeRoute: GlobalHooks["beforeRoute"] = [
  () => {
    if (process.env.MAINTENANCE === "1") {
      return new Response("Down for maintenance", { status: 503 });
    }
  },
];
```

For auth, check credentials in `transform` instead, so a caller without a token gets a 401 before validation runs. See [Auth goes in transform](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system#auth-goes-in-transform).

Returning a `Response` from `onRequest` or `beforeRoute` stops the request. The handler does not run, but `afterRoute` and `mapResponse` still do.

Hooks live in `src/hooks.ts` (every request) or in a route's `hooks.ts` (that route only). Plugins are a separate thing: they package hooks for reuse.

See [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system) for the full guide.

## Related

- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)
- [Route Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/route-specific)
- [Hooks and Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers'
---

# Providers

A provider is a service your app shares across requests: a database client, a mailer, a cache. It is created once when the app starts. Handlers read it from `ctx.services`.

## Register a provider

`src/providers.ts` default-exports a function. Call `provide(name, service)` inside it. The function may be async.

```ts title="src/providers.ts"
import type { ProviderRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { db } from "./db";

export default (burger: ProviderRegistrar) => {
  burger.provide("db", db);
};
```

A service can be any value: a class instance, an object or a function.

```ts title="src/db.ts"
export class Database {
  private users = [{ id: 1, name: "Ada" }];

  async listUsers() {
    return this.users;
  }
}

export const db = new Database();
```

## Read a provider

```ts title="src/api/users/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const users = await ctx.services.db.listUsers();
  return Response.json({ users });
}
```

`ctx.services` works the same in hooks and plugins. WebSocket handlers use `ws.services`.

## Type the service

Add your services to `BurgerServices` in `src/types.ts`. The scaffold creates this file.

```ts title="src/types.ts"
import type { Database } from "./db";

declare module "burger-api" {
  interface BurgerServices {
    db: Database;
  }
}

export {};
```

Now `ctx.services.db` is typed as `Database` everywhere.

## Services are read-only

`ctx.services` is shared by all requests and frozen. Assigning to it, like `ctx.services.db = otherDb`, throws a `TypeError`.

For per-request values, such as a request ID, use a [transform](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global#transform) hook instead.

## Providers vs plugins

| | Providers | Plugins |
|-------|-----------|---------|
| What they add | Shared services | Hooks |
| Where you register them | `src/providers.ts` | `src/plugins.ts` |
| How you read them | `ctx.services.<name>` | Fields they add to `ctx` |

A plugin cannot register a provider. If a plugin needs a database, register it in `src/providers.ts` and read `ctx.services` in the plugin's hook. See [Hooks and Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins).

## Related

- [Applications](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/applications)
- [Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/hooks)
- [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration)
- [Testing](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/testing)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/validation'
---

# Validation

Describe the request you expect with a schema. BurgerAPI checks each request against it. Bad requests get a clear error. Good data lands on `ctx.validated`, fully typed.

Schemas use [Zod](https://zod.dev/) or any [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev/) library. Put them in the route's `schema.ts`, one export per method:

```ts title="src/api/products/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  query: z.object({ limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).optional() }),
};
```

```ts title="src/api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { limit } = ctx.validated.query;
  return Response.json({ limit });
});
```

Query values arrive as text. `z.coerce.number()` turns `"50"` into `50`. You can also turn on [coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion) for the whole app.

Validation runs after `transform` and before `beforeRoute`.

## What you can validate

- `params`: path values, like `[id]`
- `query`: the query string
- `headers`: request headers
- `cookies`: cookies
- `body`: the JSON body
- `response`: what the handler returns. See [Response Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response)

## Errors

A failed check returns `422` with an RFC 9457 Problem Details body. A route with a `body` schema rejects non-JSON requests with `415`. To change the error, handle `ValidationError` in an `onError` hook. See [Validation Errors](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/errors).

## Related

- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query)
- [Body Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/body)
- [Coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion)
- [Response Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration'
---

# Configuration

Settings live in a few files, each for one job:

| File | What it sets |
|------|--------------|
| `src/index.ts` | Your app: `new Burger({...})` with the route folders and prefixes |
| `src/openapi.config.ts` | API docs: title, version, servers, docs page |
| `src/plugins.ts` | Which plugins run |
| `src/providers.ts` | Shared services, such as a database client |
| `api/**/config.ts` | Settings for one route, such as `auth` |
| `burger.build.ts` | Settings for the CLI when it builds and checks your project |

## App

```typescript title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const burger = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
  apiPrefix: "/api",
});

burger.serve(4000);
```

Folder paths can be relative to the project root (`./src/api`) or to `src/` (`api`). If a folder is not found, the error lists the paths that were tried.

## API docs

```typescript title="src/openapi.config.ts"
import type { OpenAPIConfig } from "burger-api";

export default {
  title: "My Burger API",
  version: "1.0.0",
  description: "An API built with BurgerAPI",
  servers: [{ url: "https://api.example.com", description: "Production" }],
} satisfies OpenAPIConfig;
```

See [OpenAPI](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/openapi) for every field.

## Build settings

```typescript title="burger.build.ts"
export default {
  apiDir: "./src/api",
  apiPrefix: "/api",
  debug: false,
};
```

`burger-api create` writes this file. The CLI reads it when it builds or checks your project; your running app does not. Keep `apiDir` and `apiPrefix` the same here and in `src/index.ts`. `burger-api doctor` warns when they differ.

## Plugins and providers

`src/plugins.ts` registers plugins with `burger.usePlugin()`. See [Hooks and Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins).

`src/providers.ts` registers shared services with `burger.provide()`. Handlers read them from `ctx.services`. See [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers).

## Route settings

A route's `config.ts` holds settings for that route. Plugins and hooks read them from `ctx.config`:

```typescript title="src/api/admin/config.ts"
export default {
  auth: { required: true, roles: ["admin"] },
};
```

To change a setting for one method, export it by method name:

```typescript title="src/api/items/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };

export const POST = { auth: { required: true } };
```

Here GET is public and POST needs a logged-in user.

A route folder's `config.ts` applies to that route only, not to folders below it. The framework itself reads one key, `responseValidation`. See [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration).

To type your own keys, add them to `RouteConfig` in `src/types.ts`:

```typescript title="src/types.ts"
declare module "burger-api" {
  interface RouteConfig {
    auth?: boolean | { required?: boolean; roles?: string[] };
  }
}
```

## Environment variables

Bun loads `.env` files on its own, so you do not need a loader. To check that required variables are set, use the [env plugin](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/env).

## Types

All from `burger-api`:

- `ServerOptions`: the `new Burger({...})` options
- `OpenAPIConfig`: `src/openapi.config.ts`
- `BuildConfig`: `burger.build.ts`
- `RouteConfig`: `config.ts`
- `GlobalHooks`: `src/hooks.ts`

See [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety).

## Related

- [Applications](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/applications)
- [Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers)
- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core/response-types'
---

# Response Types

Handlers return a standard Web [Response](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Response). There is no custom response type.

**JSON:**

```typescript
return Response.json({ message: "Hello" });
return Response.json({ error: "Not found" }, { status: 404 });
```

**Text or HTML:**

```typescript
return new Response("OK");
return new Response("<h1>Hello</h1>", {
  headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html" },
});
```

**Custom headers:**

```typescript
return new Response(body, {
  status: 200,
  headers: { "X-Custom": "value" },
});
```

To set status or headers from a hook, use `ctx.set`. See [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation). For what hooks can return, see [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types).

## Related

- [Handlers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/handlers)
- [Request Context](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/request-handling)
- [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation)
- [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing'
---

# File-Based Routing

In BurgerAPI, folders under your `apiDir` become URL paths. A `route.ts` file in a folder defines the handlers for that path. You do not register routes by hand.

## Example

```
api/products/route.ts     ->  /api/products
api/users/[id]/route.ts   ->  /api/users/:id
```

In `route.ts`, export a function for each HTTP method you support: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and so on. JavaScript projects use `route.js` or `route.mjs`.

## Route types

- **Static routes**: fixed paths. See [Static API Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes).
- **Dynamic routes**: a `[param]` folder captures one segment. See [Dynamic Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes).
- **Wildcard routes**: a `[...]` folder matches the rest of the path. Named folders such as `[...slug]` are an error. See [Wildcard Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/wildcard-routes).
- **Route groups**: a `(folder)` organizes files without changing the URL. See [Route Groups](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/route-groups).

These nest by folder depth. See [Nested Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/nested-routes).

You do not need `HEAD` or `OPTIONS` handlers. See [Automatic HEAD](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes#automatic-head) and [Automatic OPTIONS](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes#automatic-options).

## Route collisions

API routes, pages, assets, `/openapi.json` and `/docs` share one URL space. If two of them resolve to the same path, the app fails at startup with an error that names both. Rename one of them.

## Types

Handlers take one argument, `BurgerContext`. If the route has a `schema.ts`, wrap the handler with `defineRoute` to get typed `ctx.validated`:

```typescript title="api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  ctx.validated.query; // typed from schema.ts
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
});
```

See [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety).

## Related

- [Static API Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes)
- [Dynamic Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes)
- [Wildcard Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/wildcard-routes)
- [Static Pages](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/pages/static-pages)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes'
---

# Static API Routes

A static route has a fixed path, such as `/api/products`. It captures no values from the URL.

## Create a route

Put a `route.ts` file in a folder under your `apiDir`. The folder path becomes the URL. The default `apiPrefix` is `api`.

```
api/
  products/
    route.ts           -> /api/products
    featured/
      route.ts         -> /api/products/featured
  users/
    profile/
      route.ts         -> /api/users/profile
```

In `route.ts`, export one function per HTTP method. Use uppercase names: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`.

```typescript title="api/products/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ message: "Fetched products" });
}

export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const body = await ctx.json();
  return Response.json({ created: body }, { status: 201 });
}
```

Each handler gets one argument, `ctx` (a `BurgerContext`), and must return a standard `Response`. Returning a plain object does not work. See [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api) for what `ctx` holds.

For a full example with GET and POST, see [CRUD API](https://burger-api.com/docs/examples/crud-api).

## Which route wins

When several routes could match a URL, the most specific one wins:

1. Static (`featured/`)
2. Dynamic (`[id]/`)
3. Wildcard (`[...]/`)

```
api/products/featured/route.ts   -> GET /api/products/featured
api/products/[id]/route.ts       -> GET /api/products/123
api/products/[...]/route.ts      -> GET /api/products/123/reviews
```

## Built-in method handling

### Method Not Allowed (405)

If a route exists but does not export the requested method, the response is `405` with an `Allow` header:

```
DELETE /api/products   -> 405  Allow: GET, HEAD, POST, OPTIONS
```

### Automatic HEAD

You do not write a `HEAD` handler. A `HEAD` request runs your `GET` handler and sends no body.

### Automatic OPTIONS

Every route answers `OPTIONS` with `204` and an `Allow` header. The automatic handler skips `transform` and `beforeRoute`, so auth checks do not block CORS preflight requests. If you export your own `OPTIONS` handler, it replaces the automatic one.

### Trailing slash

`/api/products/` matches `/api/products`.

## Types

Type the handler parameter with `BurgerContext`:

```typescript
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ message: "ok" });
}
```

For typed query, params or body, add a `schema.ts` and wrap the handler with `defineRoute`. See [Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod) and [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety).

## Related

- [Dynamic Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes)
- [Wildcard Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/wildcard-routes)
- [Route Groups](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/route-groups)
- [File-Based Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/route-groups'
---

# Route Groups

A route group is a folder name in parentheses, such as `(admin)`. It helps you organize files. It does not appear in the URL.

## Example

```
api/
  (public)/
    products/
      route.ts         -> /api/products
  (admin)/
    users/
      route.ts         -> /api/users
      [userId]/
        route.ts       -> /api/users/:userId
```

The URL is `/api/users`, not `/api/admin/users`. Groups work with dynamic and wildcard folders, and you can nest them.

| Folder | In the URL? | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `(admin)/users/` | No | `/api/users` |
| `admin/users/` | Yes | `/api/admin/users` |

## Rules to know

### Groups do not apply files to their children

A group only changes the URL. A `hooks.ts` or `config.ts` inside `(admin)/` does not apply to the routes in it. Routes never inherit files from parent folders.

Put `hooks.ts` and `config.ts` next to each `route.ts` they should affect. To protect many routes at once, use a plugin or a global hook.

If a folder has convention files but no `route.ts`, BurgerAPI prints a startup warning:

```
[burger-api] (authenticated) has config.ts, hooks.ts but no route.ts, so they apply to nothing.
```

### Two routes cannot share a URL

Groups are removed from the path, so the same route in two groups gives the same URL. The app fails at startup:

```
api/(v1)/users/route.ts   -> /api/users
api/(v2)/users/route.ts   -> /api/users   ❌ startup error
```

If the version should be in the URL, use a normal folder: `api/v1/users/route.ts` -> `/api/v1/users`.

## Related

- [Static Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes)
- [Dynamic Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes)
- [Wildcard Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/wildcard-routes)
- [File-Based Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes'
---

# Dynamic Routes

A dynamic route captures part of the URL, such as an ID or a slug. Name a folder with square brackets: `[id]`. The value is in `ctx.params.id`.

## Example

```
api/
  products/
    [id]/
      route.ts         -> /api/products/:id
```

```typescript title="api/products/[id]/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const { id } = ctx.params;
  return Response.json({ productId: id });
}
```

```
GET /api/products/123      -> ctx.params.id = "123"
GET /api/products/abc-def  -> ctx.params.id = "abc-def"
```

Values are always strings. Convert them yourself (for example `Number(id)`), or use a schema with coercion.

## Several parameters

Each `[name]` folder adds a key to `ctx.params`:

```
api/users/[userId]/posts/[postId]/route.ts   -> /api/users/:userId/posts/:postId
```

```typescript
const { userId, postId } = ctx.params;
// GET /api/users/42/posts/789 -> userId = "42", postId = "789"
```

## Validate parameters

Add a `params` schema in `schema.ts`. Invalid values get a `422` response before your handler runs. Use `defineRoute` to get `ctx.validated.params` typed from the schema.

```typescript title="api/products/[id]/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  params: z.object({
    id: z.string().uuid(),
  }),
};
```

```typescript title="api/products/[id]/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { id } = ctx.validated.params; // typed: string
  return Response.json({ productId: id });
});
```

`ctx.params` is the raw `Record<string, string>`. Use `ctx.validated.params` when you want typed, checked values. See [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod).

## Rules to know

- **Static wins over dynamic.** With `products/featured/` and `products/[id]/`, `/api/products/featured` goes to the static route. Order is static, then `[param]`, then `[...]`.
- **One parameter name per level.** `[id]/` and `[productId]/` in the same folder is a startup error. Pick one name.
- **A parameter matches one segment.** `/api/products/1/reviews` does not match `[id]`. Use a [wildcard](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/wildcard-routes) for many segments.
- **No empty values.** `/api/products/` does not match `[id]` with an empty string. It matches `/api/products` if that route exists.

## Related

- [Static Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes)
- [Wildcard Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/wildcard-routes)
- [Route Groups](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/route-groups)
- [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/wildcard-routes'
---

# Wildcard Routes

A wildcard route matches every path below a point in the URL. Name a folder `[...]`. The captured segments are in `ctx.wildcardParams`, an array of strings.

## Example

```
api/
  files/
    [...]/
      route.ts         -> /api/files/*
```

```typescript title="api/files/[...]/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const segments = ctx.wildcardParams;

  if (segments.length === 0) {
    return Response.json({ error: "No file path" }, { status: 400 });
  }

  return Response.json({ path: segments.join("/") });
}
```

```
GET /api/files                         -> wildcardParams = []
GET /api/files/report.pdf              -> wildcardParams = ["report.pdf"]
GET /api/files/docs/2024/report.pdf    -> wildcardParams = ["docs", "2024", "report.pdf"]
```

The wildcard also matches its base path (`/api/files`) with an empty array. Check `segments.length` if you need to handle that case.

## With a dynamic segment

You can put a wildcard under a `[param]` folder. Validate the param with a schema. Check the wildcard segments yourself: schemas do not validate them.

```
api/users/[userId]/[...]/route.ts   -> /api/users/:userId/*
```

```typescript title="api/users/[userId]/[...]/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const { userId } = ctx.params;
  const rest = ctx.wildcardParams;
  // GET /api/users/123/posts/456 -> userId = "123", rest = ["posts", "456"]
  return Response.json({ userId, rest });
}
```

## Rules to know

- **Use `[...]` only.** A named folder such as `[...slug]` is an error in dev and in builds. Read `ctx.wildcardParams` instead.
- **Wildcards match last.** Order is static, then `[param]`, then `[...]`. A wildcard only gets requests no other route matches.
- **A wildcard must be the last folder.** A folder after `[...]`, or two wildcards at the same level, fails at startup.
- **Not typed by name.** `ctx.wildcardParams` is always `string[]`. If you need named, typed values, use [dynamic segments](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes).

Example of the order:

```
api/admin/settings/route.ts    -> /api/admin/settings
api/admin/[section]/route.ts   -> /api/admin/users
api/admin/[...]/route.ts       -> /api/admin/users/list
```

## Related

- [Static Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes)
- [Dynamic Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes)
- [Route Groups](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/route-groups)
- [File-Based Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/nested-routes'
---

# Nested Routes

Each folder under your `apiDir` adds one segment to the URL. You can mix static folders, [dynamic segments](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes) and [route groups](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/route-groups) at any depth.

## Example

```
api/users/route.ts                     ->  /api/users
api/users/[id]/route.ts                ->  /api/users/:id
api/users/[id]/posts/route.ts          ->  /api/users/:id/posts
api/users/[id]/posts/[postId]/route.ts ->  /api/users/:id/posts/:postId
```

A deeper route gets every parameter above it:

```typescript title="api/users/[id]/posts/[postId]/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const { id, postId } = ctx.params;
  return Response.json({ id, postId });
}
```

Each route folder is separate. A child route does not inherit `schema.ts`, `hooks.ts` or `config.ts` from its parent folder. Add the files you need next to each `route.ts`.

## Related

- [File-Based Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing)
- [Static API Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes)
- [Dynamic Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/pages/static-pages'
---

# File-Based Static Pages

BurgerAPI can also serve HTML pages. Pages use the same folder rules as API routes.

## Setup

Set `pageDir` in the `Burger` constructor:

```typescript title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const burger = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
  pageDir: "./src/pages",
  pagePrefix: "", // optional, no prefix by default
});

burger.serve(4000);
```

## How files map to URLs

- `src/pages/index.html` or `index.tsx` -> `/`
- `src/pages/about.html` -> `/about`
- `src/pages/products/index.html` -> `/products`
- `src/pages/(marketing)/contact.html` -> `/contact` (groups are not in the URL)
- `src/pages/posts/[slug].tsx` -> `/posts/:slug`

Two dynamic page files at the same level (`[a].tsx` and `[b].tsx`) fail at startup.

## HTML files

A `.html` file is served as-is.

```html title="src/pages/about.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <title>About Us</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>About</h1>
  </body>
</html>
```

## Dynamic pages (`.tsx`)

A `.tsx` page is a handler function, not React rendering. Its default export gets a `BurgerContext` and must return a `Response`. Returning JSX does not render anything.

```tsx title="src/pages/posts/[slug].tsx"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export default async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext): Promise<Response> {
  const slug = ctx.params.slug;
  return new Response(
    `<!doctype html><html><body><h1>Post: ${slug}</h1></body></html>`,
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html" } }
  );
}
```

## Good to know

- Pages answer `GET` and `HEAD` only. Other methods get `405`.
- Global and plugin hooks (`onRequest`, `afterRoute`, `mapResponse`) run for pages too, so CORS and security headers apply.
- Dynamic `[param]` pages work only with `serve()` on Bun. With `toFetchHandler` (Node, Cloudflare, Deno, Vercel), the app logs a warning listing the pages it cannot serve.

## Related

- [File-Based Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing)
- [Static API Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes)
- [Dynamic Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/dynamic-routes)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system'
---

# Hook System

Hooks let you run code at fixed points of a request. Use them for auth, logging, headers and error handling.

Hooks and plugins are separate things. A hook runs at one point of a request. A plugin is a package of hooks that you register in `src/plugins.ts`.

## The six hooks

| Hook | When it runs |
|------|------|
| `onRequest` | The request enters the app, before routing |
| `transform` | After routing, before validation. Adds fields to `ctx` |
| `beforeRoute` | After validation, before the handler |
| `afterRoute` | After the handler returns |
| `mapResponse` | Right before the response is sent |
| `onError` | When an error is thrown |

```
onRequest -> Routing -> transform -> Validation -> beforeRoute
  -> Handler -> afterRoute -> mapResponse
```

An error thrown in any step goes to `onError`. A request that matches no route gets a 404.

## What a hook returns

- `undefined`: continue.
- A `Response` from `onRequest` or `beforeRoute`: stop here and send this response. The handler does not run. `afterRoute` and `mapResponse` still run on it.
- A `Response` from `afterRoute` or `mapResponse`: replace the current response.
- A function `(response) => Response`: change the response.

See [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types) for details and examples.

```ts title="src/api/users/hooks.ts"
import type { RouteHooks } from "burger-api";

export const beforeRoute: RouteHooks["beforeRoute"] = [
  () => {
    if (process.env.MAINTENANCE === "1") {
      return new Response("Down for maintenance", { status: 503 });
    }
  },
];
```

## Where hooks live

- **Global**: `src/hooks.ts`. See [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global).
- **Route**: `hooks.ts` next to a `route.ts`. See [Route Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/route-specific).
- **Plugin**: the `hooks` of a plugin registered in `src/plugins.ts`. See [Hooks and Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins).

Global and plugin `afterRoute` and `mapResponse` run for every response: 404s, errors, pages, assets and `/docs` too. Route hooks run only when their route matches.

`onRequest` is not allowed in a route `hooks.ts`. It runs before routing, so put it in `src/hooks.ts` or a plugin.

Hooks are not inherited. A route's `hooks.ts` applies to that route only, not to sub-folders.

## Order

- `onRequest`, `transform`, `beforeRoute`: plugin hooks first, then global, then route.
- `afterRoute`, `mapResponse`, `onError`: route hooks first, then global, then plugin.

## Auth goes in transform

`transform` runs before validation. If you check auth there, a caller without a token gets a 401, not a 422 that lists your schema fields. Throw `UnauthorizedError` to reject. Use `beforeRoute` for checks that need `ctx.validated`.

## Changing status and headers

Set `ctx.set.status` and `ctx.set.headers` from any hook or handler. See [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation).

## Related

- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)
- [Route Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/route-specific)
- [After Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/after)
- [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types)
- [Hook Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/hook-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global'
---

# Global Hooks

Global hooks run for every request. Put them in `src/hooks.ts`, with one named export per hook.

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { cors } from "../ecosystem/hooks/cors/cors";
import { logger } from "../ecosystem/hooks/logger/logger";

export const onRequest = [logger(), cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"] })];
```

You can export any of the six hooks: `onRequest`, `transform`, `beforeRoute`, `afterRoute`, `mapResponse`, `onError`. Ready-made hooks such as `cors` and `logger` come from the [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction).

Global `onRequest`, `afterRoute` and `mapResponse` run for every response, including 404s, pages, assets and `/docs`. Global `transform` and `beforeRoute` run for matched API routes.

## transform

`transform` is an object, not a function. Each key is a field name. Each value is a function that gets `ctx` and returns the field's value. The field is added to `ctx` before validation, so later hooks and the handler can read it.

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { UnauthorizedError } from "burger-api";
import type { GlobalHooks } from "burger-api";

export const transform: GlobalHooks["transform"] = {
  user: (ctx) => {
    const token = ctx.headers.get("authorization");
    if (!token) {
      throw new UnauthorizedError("Missing token");
    }
    return { token };
  },
};
```

Rules:

- You cannot use a name that `ctx` already has, such as `params`, `query` or `set`. The app fails at startup if you do.
- A route `transform` with the same name overrides the global one.
- Add the field to `BurgerContext` in `src/types.ts` to type it. See [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers#type-the-service).

## Related

- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [Route Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/route-specific)
- [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types)
- [Request Context](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/request-handling)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/route-specific'
---

# Route Hooks

Route hooks run only for one route. Put them in a `hooks.ts` file next to the route's `route.ts`.

```ts title="src/api/users/hooks.ts"
import { ForbiddenError } from "burger-api";
import type { RouteHooks } from "burger-api";

export const transform: RouteHooks["transform"] = {
  admin: (ctx) => {
    if (ctx.query.admin !== "true") {
      throw new ForbiddenError("Admin only");
    }
    return true;
  },
};
```

A route `hooks.ts` can export `transform`, `beforeRoute`, `afterRoute`, `mapResponse` and `onError`.

- `onRequest` is not allowed here. It runs before routing, so put it in `src/hooks.ts` or a plugin. A route `onRequest` export is ignored with a warning.
- Route hooks run after global hooks for `transform` and `beforeRoute`, and before global hooks for `afterRoute`, `mapResponse` and `onError`.
- Hooks are not inherited. They apply only to their own route folder.

## Typed ctx.validated

If a hook reads `ctx.validated`, wrap the hooks with `defineHooks(schema, hooks)`. It types `ctx` from the route's schema.

```ts title="src/api/users/hooks.ts"
import { defineHooks } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const { beforeRoute } = defineHooks(GetSchema, {
  beforeRoute: (ctx) => {
    ctx.validated.query; // typed from schema.ts
  },
});
```

Route hooks run for every method of the route. A slot that only one method has, like `body`, may be `undefined`. Read it with `ctx.validated.body?.name`.

## Related

- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)
- [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types)
- [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types'
---

# Hook Return Types

A hook returns one of three things.

| Return | `onRequest`, `beforeRoute` | `afterRoute`, `mapResponse` |
|--------|----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| `undefined` | Continue | Continue |
| `Response` | Stop. Skip the handler and send this response | Replace the current response |
| `(response) => Response` | Change the response after the handler runs | Change the response now |

When a forward hook stops the request, `afterRoute` and `mapResponse` still run. So headers such as CORS still reach a 401 or 429.

`onError` returns a `Response` to handle the error, or `undefined` to let the next `onError` hook try.

```ts title="src/api/users/hooks.ts"
import type { RouteHooks } from "burger-api";

export const beforeRoute: RouteHooks["beforeRoute"] = [
  () => {
    if (process.env.MAINTENANCE === "1") {
      return new Response("Down for maintenance", { status: 503 }); // stop
    }
    return undefined; // continue
  },
];

export const afterRoute: RouteHooks["afterRoute"] = [
  () => (response) => {
    const headers = new Headers(response.headers);
    headers.set("X-Custom", "value");
    return new Response(response.body, { status: response.status, headers });
  },
];
```

## Types

Import these from `burger-api`:

- `RouteHooks`: the shape of a route `hooks.ts` (no `onRequest`).
- `GlobalHooks`: the shape of `src/hooks.ts` and plugin hooks (adds `onRequest`).
- `ForwardHook`, `ResponseHook`, `ErrorHook`: one hook function.

TypeScript rejects a wrong return value:

```ts
export const beforeRoute: RouteHooks["beforeRoute"] = [
  () => "yes", // ❌ Type 'string' is not assignable
];
```

Run `bun run typecheck` to check your code. See [Hook Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/hook-types) for the full signatures.

## Related

- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [After Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/after)
- [Hook Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/hook-types)
- [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/after'
---

# After Hooks

`afterRoute` runs after the handler returns. `mapResponse` runs right before the response is sent. Use them to change the response, for example to add headers.

Return a function from the hook. It gets the current `Response` and returns a new one.

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import type { GlobalHooks } from "burger-api";

export const afterRoute: GlobalHooks["afterRoute"] = [
  () => (response) => {
    const headers = new Headers(response.headers);
    headers.set("X-Powered-By", "BurgerAPI");
    return new Response(response.body, { status: response.status, headers });
  },
];
```

Global and plugin after hooks run for every response: matched routes, 404s, errors, pages, assets and `/docs`. Route after hooks run only for their route.

For CORS, use the [cors hook](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/cors). For a simple status or header change, `ctx.set` is often easier. See [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation).

## Related

- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)
- [Route Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/route-specific)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod'
---

# Zod Validation

BurgerAPI uses [Zod](https://zod.dev/) 4 to check requests. You write a schema in `schema.ts`. BurgerAPI checks the request before your handler runs and puts the typed result on `ctx.validated`.

You can validate `query`, `params`, `headers`, `cookies` and `body`.

```ts title="api/products/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  query: z.object({
    limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).optional(),
  }),
};
```

```ts title="api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { limit } = ctx.validated.query; // number | undefined
  return Response.json({ limit });
});
```

`defineRoute` gives `ctx.validated` the types from your schema. To reuse a slot type elsewhere, use `z.infer<typeof GET.query>`.

`z.coerce.number()` turns the text `"50"` into the number `50`. To convert text for the whole app, see [Coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion).

Other schema libraries work too. See [Standard Schema Support](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/standard-schema).

## Related

- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Params Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/params)
- [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query)
- [Body Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/body)
- [Standard Schema Support](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/standard-schema)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema'
---

# Schema Definition

Put validation schemas in `schema.ts`, next to `route.ts`. Export one object per HTTP method (`GET`, `POST`, and so on).

Validation runs after `transform` hooks and before `beforeRoute` hooks. If it fails, the request gets `422` and the handler does not run.

## The full shape

Every slot is optional. Describe only what you use.

```typescript title="api/products/[id]/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  params: z.object({ id: z.string() }),         // path params
  query: z.object({ limit: z.coerce.number() }), // query string
  headers: z.object({ "x-api-key": z.string() }),
  cookies: z.object({ session: z.string() }),
  coerce: true,                                  // convert text values
};

export const PUT = {
  params: z.object({ id: z.string() }),
  body: z.object({ name: z.string() }),          // JSON body
  response: { 200: z.object({ id: z.string() }) },
};
```

## Use the validated data

Wrap the handler with `defineRoute` to get types from the schema:

```typescript title="api/products/[id]/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { id } = ctx.validated.params;   // string
  const { limit } = ctx.validated.query; // number
  return Response.json({ id, limit });
});
```

The data is on `ctx.validated.params`, `.query`, `.headers`, `.cookies` and `.body`.

## Share a schema

Define a shape once and import it:

```typescript title="src/schemas.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const Pagination = z.object({
  page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
});
```

```typescript title="api/items/schema.ts"
import { Pagination } from "../../schemas";

export const GET = { query: Pagination };
```

## Related

- [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod)
- [Params Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/params)
- [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query)
- [Body Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/body)
- [Headers Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/headers)
- [Cookie Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/cookie)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/params'
---

# Params Validation

Add a `params` schema to check path parameters from dynamic folders such as `[id]`. The validated values are on `ctx.validated.params`.

```ts title="api/products/[id]/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = { params: z.object({ id: z.string().uuid() }) };
```

```ts title="api/products/[id]/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { id } = ctx.validated.params; // typed: string
  return Response.json({ id });
});
```

Path values are text. Turn on [coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion) for a number id.

Without a schema, `ctx.params` still holds the raw strings, but nothing checks them.

## Related

- [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod)
- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query'
---

# Query Validation

Add a `query` schema to a method in `schema.ts`. The validated values are on `ctx.validated.query`.

```ts title="api/products/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  query: z.object({
    search: z.string().optional(),
    limit: z.coerce.number().optional(),
  }),
};
```

```ts title="api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { search, limit } = ctx.validated.query; // string | undefined, number | undefined
  return Response.json({ search, limit });
});
```

Query values are text. `z.coerce.number()` turns `"10"` into `10`. You can also turn on [coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion) for the whole app.

## Related

- [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod)
- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Params Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/params)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/body'
---

# Body Validation

Add a `body` schema to a method in `schema.ts`. The validated body is on `ctx.validated.body`.

```ts title="api/products/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const POST = {
  body: z.object({ name: z.string().min(1), price: z.number().positive() }),
};
```

```ts title="api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { POST as PostSchema } from "./schema";

export const POST = defineRoute(PostSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { name, price } = ctx.validated.body; // typed from the schema
  return Response.json({ name, price }, { status: 201 });
});
```

## Rules

- The body must be JSON (`application/json` or `application/*+json`). Other content types get `415`.
- Malformed JSON gets `400`.
- A body that fails the schema gets `422`.
- An empty body validates as `undefined`, so an optional body schema still works.

## Related

- [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod)
- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Params Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/params)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/headers'
---

# Headers Validation

Add a `headers` schema to a method in `schema.ts`. The validated values are on `ctx.validated.headers`.

```typescript title="api/secure/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  headers: z.object({ "x-api-key": z.string().min(1) }),
};
```

```typescript title="api/secure/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  return Response.json({ key: ctx.validated.headers["x-api-key"] });
});
```

If the header is missing or empty, the request gets `422`.

## Good to know

- Write header keys in lowercase (`"x-api-key"`). A key with capitals is a startup error.
- Header values are text. Turn on [coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion) if you expect numbers or booleans.

## Related

- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Cookie Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/cookie)
- [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query)
- [Validation Errors](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/errors)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/cookie'
---

# Cookie Validation

Add a `cookies` schema to a method in `schema.ts`. The validated values are on `ctx.validated.cookies`.

```typescript title="api/session/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  cookies: z.object({ session: z.string().min(1) }),
};
```

```typescript title="api/session/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  return Response.json({ session: ctx.validated.cookies.session });
});
```

If the `session` cookie is missing, the request gets `422`.

Cookie values are text. Turn on [coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion) if you expect numbers or booleans.

## Related

- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Headers Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/headers)
- [Validation Errors](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/errors)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion'
---

# Coercion (Automatic Type Conversion)

Query strings, path params, headers and cookies always arrive as text. `?n=42` gives you the string `"42"`, so `z.number()` would reject it.

Coercion converts the text for you: `"42"` becomes `42`, `"true"` becomes `true`, and `"2026-01-01"` becomes a `Date`. It is off by default.

## Turn it on

For the whole app:

```typescript title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const app = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
  validation: { coerce: true },
});
```

For one method:

```typescript title="api/stats/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  query: z.object({ n: z.number(), b: z.boolean() }),
  coerce: true,
};
```

For every method in one `schema.ts`:

```typescript title="api/stats/schema.ts"
export const coerce = true;

export const GET = { query: z.object({ n: z.number() }) };
```

Now `?n=42&b=true` gives `ctx.validated.query` the value `{ n: 42, b: true }`.

## What gets converted

| Schema field | Converts to |
|--------------|-------------|
| `z.number()` | number |
| `z.boolean()` | boolean (`"true"`/`"1"` and `"false"`/`"0"`) |
| `z.date()` | `Date` |
| `z.array(z.number())` | array of numbers |

## Good to know

- Coercion works on `query`, `params`, `headers` and `cookies`. It does not touch the JSON body.
- It works with Zod schemas. For other schema libraries, use that library's own conversion.
- A value that cannot be converted fails validation with `422`.
- You can still use Zod's `z.coerce.number()` on a single field.

## Related

- [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod)
- [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query)
- [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration)
- [Validation Best Practices](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/best-practices)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response'
---

# Response Validation

Add a `response` schema to check what your handler returns. Only JSON responses are checked (`application/json` and `application/*+json`).

```typescript title="api/status/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = {
  response: { 200: z.object({ ok: z.boolean() }) },
};
```

```typescript title="api/status/route.ts"
export function GET() {
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}
```

## Modes

- **`dev`** (default): in development, a mismatch is logged. The response is sent unchanged.
- **`enforce`**: a mismatch becomes a `500` problem+json response. Production hides the issues. `afterRoute` and `mapResponse` still run, so headers such as CORS stay.
- **`off`**: responses are not checked.

Set the app-wide mode with `validation.responseValidation`. Override it for one route in `config.ts`:

```typescript title="src/api/reports/config.ts"
export default {
  responseValidation: "enforce",
};
```

## Status keys

Key each schema by status code (`200`) or status class (`2xx`). An exact code wins over a class. Any other key is a startup error.

## Related

- [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration)
- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Problem Details](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/problem-details)
- [Validation Best Practices](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/best-practices)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/standard-schema'
---

# Standard Schema Support

You can use any schema library that follows [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev/), such as [Valibot](https://valibot.dev/) or [ArkType](https://arktype.io/). Use it in `schema.ts` the same way as Zod. No setup is needed.

```typescript title="api/products/schema.ts"
import { object, string, number } from "valibot";

export const POST = {
  body: object({ name: string(), price: number() }),
};
```

```typescript title="api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { POST as PostSchema } from "./schema";

export const POST = defineRoute(PostSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { name, price } = ctx.validated.body;
  return Response.json({ name, price });
});
```

## Good to know

- The validator must be synchronous. An async validator is a startup error.
- A schema that is neither Zod nor Standard Schema is a startup error.
- You can mix Zod and other libraries in one app.
- Built-in [coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion) works with Zod only. Use your library's own conversion.

## Related

- [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod)
- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/errors'
---

# Validation Error Handling

When a request fails validation, BurgerAPI answers `422`. The handler does not run.

## Default body

The default body follows RFC 9457 (`application/problem+json`). Issues are grouped by slot (`query`, `params`, `headers`, `cookies`, `body`):

```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "query: Invalid input: expected number, received string",
  "errors": {
    "query": [
      {
        "path": ["limit"],
        "message": "Invalid input: expected number, received string",
        "code": "invalid_type"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

See [Problem Details](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/problem-details) for each field.

## Plain body

Set `errorFormat: "plain"` in [configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration) to send only the `errors` object:

```json
{
  "errors": {
    "query": [{ "path": ["limit"], "message": "Invalid input: expected number, received string", "code": "invalid_type" }]
  }
}
```

## Custom body

Pass an `errorRenderer` in [configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration) to build the response yourself.

Production error bodies never include stack traces or source paths.

## Related

- [Zod Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/zod)
- [Problem Details](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/problem-details)
- [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration)
- [Validation Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/problem-details'
---

# Problem Details (problem+json)

By default, a failed request gets a `422` with an `application/problem+json` body. The shape follows [RFC 9457](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457). You do not need to turn it on.

## The response shape

For `GET /api/items?limit=abc` with `query: z.object({ limit: z.number() })`:

```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "query: Invalid input: expected number, received string",
  "errors": {
    "query": [
      {
        "path": ["limit"],
        "message": "Invalid input: expected number, received string",
        "code": "invalid_type"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

- `title`: `"Validation Error"` for validation failures. Other errors use the status phrase, such as `"Not Found"`.
- `detail`: the slot and the first message, or the number of errors.
- `errors`: issues grouped by slot. Each issue has a `path`, a `message`, and for Zod a `code`.

Production bodies never include stack traces or source paths. In development, extra details such as `stack` may appear.

To use a simpler body, set `errorFormat: "plain"`. To build your own, pass an `errorRenderer`. See [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration).

## Related

- [Validation Errors](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/errors)
- [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration)
- [Response Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration'
---

# Validation Configuration

Set validation options with the `validation` option of `new Burger()`.

```typescript title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const app = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
  validation: {
    coerce: true,
    responseValidation: "dev",
    errorFormat: "problem+json",
  },
});
```

| Option | Values | Default | What it does |
|--------|--------|---------|--------------|
| `coerce` | `boolean` | `false` | Convert text in query, params, headers and cookies. See [Coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion). |
| `responseValidation` | `"off"` \| `"dev"` \| `"enforce"` | `"dev"` | How response schemas are checked. See [Response Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response). |
| `errorFormat` | `"plain"` \| `"problem+json"` | `"problem+json"` | Shape of the error body. |
| `status` | `number` | `422` | Status for request validation failures. |
| `errorRenderer` | `(result, { slot, status }) => Response` | none | Build the error response yourself. |

A custom renderer:

```typescript title="src/index.ts"
const app = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
  validation: {
    errorRenderer: (result, { status }) =>
      Response.json({ ok: false, issues: result.issues }, { status }),
  },
});
```

A route can override `responseValidation` in its `config.ts`.

## Related

- [Coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion)
- [Response Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response)
- [Problem Details](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/problem-details)
- [Server Options](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/server-options)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/best-practices'
---

# Validation Best Practices

A few habits that keep validation simple.

- **Start small.** Add a schema only for the slots your handler reads.
- **Turn on coercion for text inputs.** Query, params, headers and cookies are text. Use [coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion) when you expect numbers or booleans.
- **Share shapes.** Define a shape once in its own file and import it into each `schema.ts`. See [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema).
- **Keep handlers thin.** The handler runs only after validation passes. Use `ctx.validated` and skip extra type checks.
- **Add response schemas.** In the default `dev` mode they only log mismatches. Use `enforce` only on routes where a wrong shape must never reach the client. See [Response Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response).
- **Pick an error format.** The default body is RFC 9457 problem details. Set `errorFormat: "plain"` for a simpler body. See [Problem Details](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/problem-details).

```typescript title="api/orders/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const POST = {
  body: z.object({ name: z.string().min(1), price: z.number() }),
};
```

## Related

- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Coercion](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/coercion)
- [Response Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/response)
- [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/websocket/overview'
---

# WebSocket

WebSocket routes keep a connection open so the server and client can send messages both ways. Use them for chat, live updates, and notifications.

## Create a route

Add a folder under `src/websocket/`. The folder path becomes the URL. Put a `ws.ts` file inside with three handlers: `open`, `message`, and `close`.

```ts
// src/websocket/chat/ws.ts  ->  ws://localhost:4000/chat
import type { BurgerWS } from "burger-api";

export function open(ws: BurgerWS) {
    ws.send("connected");
}

export function message(ws: BurgerWS, message: string | Buffer) {
    ws.send(message); // echo
}

export function close(ws: BurgerWS, code: number, reason: string) {
    // connection closed
}
```

The dev server finds the route on its own. No registration is needed.

Next to `ws.ts` you can add:

- `hooks.ts`: `onOpen`, `onMessage`, `onClose` hooks for this route.
- `config.ts`: route options. If you use an auth plugin, set `auth: false` to make the route public.

Folder names work like API routes: `[roomId]` is a parameter and `[...]` is a wildcard.

## Register a route in code

You can also add a route with `burger.websocket()`. Set connection options for the whole server with `burger.wsConfig()`:

```ts
burger.websocket("/chat", {
    open(ws) {
        ws.send("connected");
    },
    message(ws, message) {
        ws.send(message);
    },
});

burger.wsConfig({
    maxPayloadLength: 1024 * 1024, // 1 MB
    idleTimeout: 30, // seconds
});
```

## What is on `ws`

Each handler gets a `BurgerWS` object:

- `ws.send(message)`: send a string or a `Buffer`.
- `ws.close(code?, reason?)`: close the connection.
- `ws.params`: route parameters, for example `ws.params.roomId`.
- `ws.wildcardParams`: wildcard segments.
- `ws.query` and `ws.url`: the query string and URL the client connected with.
- `ws.data`: your own data for this connection.
- `ws.services`: services from `src/providers.ts`, the same as `ctx.services`.
- `ws.user`: the user set by an auth plugin.

Messages for one connection arrive in order. The first `message` runs only after `open` finishes, so an `async open` is safe.

## Reject a connection

Check the query in `open`. Close with code `1008` when it is not valid:

```ts
export function open(ws: BurgerWS) {
    const roomId = ws.query.get("roomId");
    if (!roomId) {
        ws.close(1008, "Missing roomId");
        return;
    }
    ws.data.roomId = roomId;
}
```

## Type `ws.data`

`ws.data` starts empty. Declare your fields once, usually in `src/types.ts`:

```ts
declare module "burger-api" {
    interface WebSocketData {
        roomId?: string;
    }
}
```

TypeScript now checks every read and write of `ws.data`. Services and `ws.user` use the same pattern with `BurgerServices` and `BurgerAuthUser`. See [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety).

## Pub/sub

A connection can join a topic and send a message to everyone else in that topic:

```ts
export function open(ws: BurgerWS) {
    ws.subscribe("room:general");
}

export function message(ws: BurgerWS, message: string | Buffer) {
    ws.publish("room:general", message); // the sender does not get it
}
```

A connection leaves all its topics when it closes.

To send to a topic from an HTTP route, use `ctx.publish`. It reaches every subscriber:

```ts
// src/api/announce/route.ts
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
    ctx.publish("room:general", "server announcement");
    return Response.json({ ok: true });
}
```

:::warning Bun only
`ws.subscribe`, `ws.publish`, and `ctx.publish` work only on Bun. They throw on Node.js, Cloudflare Workers, and Deno. On those runtimes, keep your own set of connections and loop over it:

```ts
const clients = new Set<BurgerWS>();

export function open(ws: BurgerWS) {
    clients.add(ws);
}

export function message(ws: BurgerWS, message: string | Buffer) {
    for (const client of clients) {
        if (client !== ws) client.send(message);
    }
}

export function close(ws: BurgerWS) {
    clients.delete(ws);
}
```
:::

## Runtime support

| Runtime | WebSocket |
|---|---|
| Bun | Yes |
| Node.js | Yes, with `@burger-api/node-server` |
| Cloudflare Workers | Yes |
| Deno | Yes |
| Vercel | No |

Your `ws.ts` files work the same on every supported runtime. Only pub/sub is Bun-only.

### Node.js

Install `@burger-api/node-server` and build with `burger-api build --target=node`. WebSocket routes work with no extra setup. See [Deploy on Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node).

### Vercel

Vercel does not support WebSocket. `burger-api build --target=vercel` fails if your project has WebSocket routes. Host the WebSocket routes on another target and call that service from your Vercel app.

## Related

- [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety)
- [Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing)
- [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility)
- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [Deploy on Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node)

# OpenAPI & Swagger

BurgerAPI builds an [OpenAPI 3.1](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0) document from your routes and schemas. You get:

- the spec at `/openapi.json`
- an interactive docs UI at `/docs`

The spec comes from your code, so it stays in sync as the API changes.

## Document metadata

Set the title, version and more in `src/openapi.config.ts`. `burger-api create` adds this file for you.

```ts title="src/openapi.config.ts"
import type { OpenAPIConfig } from "burger-api";

export default {
  title: "Widget Management API",
  description: "API for creating, reading, updating, and deleting widgets.",
  version: "1.0.2",
  servers: [{ url: "https://api.example.com", description: "Production" }],
  contact: { name: "Widget Team", email: "api@example.com" },
} satisfies OpenAPIConfig;
```

| Field | Type | Purpose |
|-------|------|---------|
| `title` | `string` | API title. Default "Burger API" |
| `description` | `string` | API description. Default "Burger API documentation" |
| `version` | `string` | API version. Default "1.0.0" |
| `servers` | `OpenAPIServer[]` | Server URLs (`{ url, description? }`) |
| `contact` | `OpenAPIContact` | `{ name?, url?, email? }` |
| `license` | `OpenAPILicense` | `{ name, url? }` |
| `termsOfService` | `string` | URL to the terms of service |
| `externalDocs` | `OpenAPIExternalDocs` | `{ url, description? }` |
| `security` | `Array<Record<string, string[]>>` | Root security requirements. Default `[]` |
| `path` | `string` | Path of the JSON spec. Default `/openapi.json` |
| `docsPath` | `string` | Path of the docs UI. Default `/docs` |
| `enabled` | `boolean` | Serve the spec and docs. Default `true` |
| `docsAuth` | `DocsAuth` | Basic auth for the docs and spec (`{ username, password }`). Omit for none |
| `provider` | `DocsProvider` | Docs UI. Default Swagger UI. Others: `scalarDocs()`, `redocDocs()` |
| `mapJsonSchema` | `Record<string, JsonSchemaConverter>` | Converters for schema libraries that cannot describe themselves, such as Valibot |

Apps without the convention file can pass the same object as `new Burger({ openapi: { ... } })`. The older `new Burger({ title, version, description })` options also work. `openapi.config.ts` wins when both exist.

## Route metadata

Add details per endpoint in the route's `openapi.ts`, with one export per method:

```ts title="src/api/products/[id]/openapi.ts"
export const GET = {
  summary: "Get a specific product by ID",
  tags: ["Products"],
  operationId: "getProductById",
  responses: {
    200: { description: "Product details returned successfully" },
    404: { description: "Product not found" },
  },
};
```

Allowed fields: `summary`, `description`, `tags`, `operationId`, `deprecated`, `responses`, `externalDocs`. Request and response schemas come from `schema.ts`, so you do not repeat them.

## Docs UI

Pick the UI with the `provider` field. The options are exported from `burger-api`: `swaggerDocs()` (default), `scalarDocs()`, `redocDocs()`.

```ts title="src/openapi.config.ts"
import { scalarDocs } from "burger-api";
import type { OpenAPIConfig } from "burger-api";

export default {
  title: "My API",
  provider: scalarDocs(),
  docsAuth: { username: "admin", password: "secret" },
} satisfies OpenAPIConfig;
```

## Related

- [Applications](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/applications)
- [Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/routing)
- [Handlers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/handlers)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/examples/basic-route'

# Basic Route Example

A route that answers `GET /api/hello`:

```typescript title="src/api/hello/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ message: "Hello, Burger API!" });
}
```

The handler gets `ctx` and returns a standard `Response`. Use `ctx` to read the query, params, body, headers and cookies. See [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api) and [Static API Routes](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/api/static-routes).
