# Hooks and Plugins

The ecosystem has two kinds of packages. They are separate ideas.

- Need code to run around requests, like headers or logging? Use a **hook**.
- Need an app feature, like auth or env checks? Use a **plugin**.

## Hooks

A hook runs at a lifecycle point: `onRequest`, `transform`, `beforeRoute`, `afterRoute`, `mapResponse` or `onError`. Add ecosystem hooks in `src/hooks.ts` (every request) or in a route's `hooks.ts` (that route only):

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { cors } from "../ecosystem/hooks/cors/cors";

export const onRequest = [cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"] })];
```

## Plugins

A plugin is `{ name, hooks? }`. Register plugins in `src/plugins.ts`:

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { apiKey } from "../ecosystem/plugins/api-key/api-key";

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(apiKey({ keys: ["demo-api-key-123"] }));
};
```

Plugins add hooks only. Services go in `src/providers.ts` with `burger.provide()`.

To register the same plugin twice (for example two JWT plugins with different secrets), pass a third `seed` argument: `usePlugin(plugin, undefined, "admin")`.

## Write your own plugin

This plugin adds `ctx.tenant` to every request:

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { Plugin, PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";

declare module "burger-api" {
  interface BurgerContext {
    tenant: string;
  }
}

const tenant: Plugin = {
  name: "tenant",
  hooks: {
    transform: {
      tenant: (ctx) => ctx.headers.get("x-tenant") ?? "public",
    },
  },
};

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(tenant);
};
```

## Related

- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)
- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [CLI Add](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/add)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/cors'
---

# CORS Hook

This hook adds `Access-Control-*` headers, so browsers can call your API from another origin. It also answers `OPTIONS` preflight requests with `204`.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add cors
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add cors --force`.

## Add it

Add it to `onRequest` in `src/hooks.ts`, so it runs before routing:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { cors } from "../ecosystem/hooks/cors/cors";

export const onRequest = [
  cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"], credentials: true }),
];
```

## Options

- `origin`: `"*"`, a string, an array or a function. Default `"*"`. With `credentials: true`, list the origins.
- `credentials`: allow cookies and auth headers.
- `methods`: allowed HTTP methods.
- `allowedHeaders`, `exposedHeaders`: header lists.
- `maxAge`: how long browsers cache the preflight, in seconds.

The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/cors/README.md`.

## Related

- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)
- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/logger'
---

# Logger Hook

This hook logs each request with its method, URL, status and response time.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add logger
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add logger --force`.

## Add it

Add it to `onRequest` in `src/hooks.ts`, so it logs every response, including 404s and errors:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { logger } from "../ecosystem/hooks/logger/logger";

export const onRequest = [logger()];
```

For options, use `createLogger()`:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { createLogger } from "../ecosystem/hooks/logger/logger";

export const onRequest = [
  createLogger({ format: "json", skip: /^\/(health|metrics)/ }),
];
```

## Options

- `format`: `"text"` or `"json"`.
- `colors`: color the output. Default `true`.
- `skip`: a string, regex or function. Matching paths are not logged.
- `requestId`: add a request ID, available as `ctx.requestId`. Default `true`.
- `logFn`: send log lines somewhere else, such as a file or a log service.

The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/logger/README.md`.

## Related

- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)
- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/rate-limiter'
---

# Rate Limiter

This hook limits how many requests a client can make in a time window. Extra requests get `429 Too Many Requests`.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add rate-limiter
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add rate-limiter --force`.

## Add it

Add it to `onRequest` in `src/hooks.ts`, so every request counts, including 404s and pages:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { rateLimit } from "../ecosystem/hooks/rate-limiter/rate-limiter";

export const onRequest = [rateLimit()]; // 100 requests per minute per client
```

A custom limit, keyed by API key:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
export const onRequest = [
  rateLimit({
    windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
    maxRequests: 50,
    keyGenerator: (ctx) => ctx.headers.get("X-API-Key") || "anonymous",
  }),
];
```

## Options

- `windowMs`: window length in milliseconds. Default `60000`.
- `maxRequests`: requests allowed per window. Default `100`.
- `keyGenerator`: how to identify a client. Default `ctx.ip`.
- `trustProxy`: read the client IP from `X-Forwarded-For`. Default `false`. Turn it on only behind a proxy you trust.

The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/rate-limiter/README.md`.

## Good to know

- Responses include `X-RateLimit-*` headers, and `Retry-After` when the limit is hit.
- Counts are kept in memory. They reset on restart and are not shared between servers.

## Related

- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)
- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/cache'
---

# Cache Hook

This hook sets the `Cache-Control` header, so browsers and CDNs know how long they may keep a response. It does not store responses itself.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add cache
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add cache --force`.

## Add it

Add it to `beforeRoute`, in `src/hooks.ts` or in a route's `hooks.ts`:

```ts title="api/products/hooks.ts"
import { publicCache } from "../../../ecosystem/hooks/cache/cache";

export const beforeRoute = [publicCache(3600)]; // Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
```

Presets:

- `noCache()`
- `publicCache(maxAge = 3600)`
- `privateCache(maxAge = 300)`
- `immutableCache()`
- `cdnCache(browserMaxAge = 300, cdnMaxAge = 3600)`

## Options

For full control, use `cacheControl()`:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { cacheControl } from "../ecosystem/hooks/cache/cache";

export const beforeRoute = [
  cacheControl({ directive: "public", maxAge: 300, sMaxAge: 3600, etag: true }),
];
```

- `directive`: `"public"`, `"private"`, `"no-cache"`, `"no-store"` or `"must-revalidate"`. Default `"no-cache"`.
- `maxAge`: browser cache time in seconds.
- `sMaxAge`: CDN cache time in seconds.
- `etag`: add an `ETag` and answer `304` when it matches. Default `false`.
- `vary`: header names to add to `Vary`.

The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/cache/README.md`.

Set cache headers in one place: global or per route, not both.

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/compression'
---

# Compression Hook

This hook compresses responses with gzip or deflate when the client accepts it. Use it to shrink JSON, HTML and other text.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add compression
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add compression --force`.

## Add it

Add it to `onRequest` in `src/hooks.ts`, so it covers every response, including errors:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { compress } from "../ecosystem/hooks/compression/compression";

export const onRequest = [compress()];
```

With no options it compresses bodies of 1KB or more.

## Options

- `threshold`: minimum body size in bytes. Default `1024`.
- `encodings`: encodings in order of preference. Default `["gzip", "deflate"]`. Brotli is not supported.
- `contentTypes`: only compress these types (string array or regex).
- `excludeContentTypes`: never compress these types. Default images, video, audio and fonts.

The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/compression/README.md`.

## Good to know

- Event streams and responses with `Content-Encoding` already set are skipped.
- If a CDN in front of your app already compresses, leave this hook off.

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/security-headers'
---

# Security Headers Hook

This hook adds response headers that protect browsers from common attacks, such as HSTS, `X-Frame-Options` and an optional Content Security Policy (CSP).

## Install

```bash
burger-api add security-headers
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add security-headers --force`.

## Add it

Add it to `onRequest` in `src/hooks.ts`, so every response gets the headers:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { securityHeaders } from "../ecosystem/hooks/security-headers/security-headers";

export const onRequest = [securityHeaders()];
```

Presets:

- `strictSecurity()`: a `'self'`-only CSP, long HSTS with `preload`, and blocks camera, microphone, location and payment.
- `relaxedSecurity()`: no CSP, no HSTS, and allows same-origin framing.

## Options

Add your own CSP with camelCase directive names:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
export const onRequest = [
  securityHeaders({
    contentSecurityPolicy: {
      defaultSrc: ["'self'"],
      scriptSrc: ["'self'", "https://cdn.example.com"],
    },
  }),
];
```

- `contentSecurityPolicy`: CSP directives. Not set by default.
- `strictTransportSecurity`: `{ maxAge, includeSubDomains, preload }`.
- `frameOptions`: `"DENY"` or `"SAMEORIGIN"`. Default `"DENY"`.
- `referrerPolicy`: default `"no-referrer"`.

Pass `false` for any option to leave that header out. The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/security-headers/README.md`.

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/timeout'
---

# Timeout Hook

This package limits how long a request may take. It has two exports:

- `withTimeout()` wraps one handler and answers `504` at the deadline.
- `requestTimeout()` is a hook for the whole app. It replaces a late response with `408`.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add timeout
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add timeout --force`.

## Wrap a handler

```ts title="src/api/report/route.ts"
import { withTimeout } from "../../../ecosystem/hooks/timeout/timeout";

export const GET = withTimeout(
  async (ctx, signal) => {
    const res = await fetch("https://slow.example.com/data", { signal });
    return Response.json(await res.json());
  },
  { ms: 5000 }
);
```

The handler gets an `AbortSignal`. Pass it to `fetch` and other work, so the work stops at the deadline too.

## Add an app-wide limit

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { requestTimeout } from "../ecosystem/hooks/timeout/timeout";

export const beforeRoute = [requestTimeout({ ms: 30000 })];
```

This hook cannot stop a slow handler. The client gets the `408` only after the handler finishes. Use `withTimeout()` when the client must get an answer on time.

## Options

- `ms`: timeout in milliseconds. Default `30000`.
- `message`: message in the default JSON body.
- `onTimeout`: a function that returns your own response.

The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/timeout/README.md`.

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/body-size-limiter'
---

# Body Size Limiter

This hook rejects request bodies that are too large. Use it on any app that accepts uploads or JSON.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add body-size-limiter
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add body-size-limiter --force`.

## Add it

Add it to `onRequest`, so it runs before anything reads the body:

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
import { bodySizeLimiter } from "../ecosystem/hooks/body-size-limiter/body-size-limiter";

export const onRequest = [bodySizeLimiter({ maxSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024 })]; // 10MB
```

With no options the limit is 1MB. A body over the limit gets `413`.

## Options

- `maxSize`: limit in bytes. Default `1048576` (1MB).
- `mode`: `"header"` or `"stream"`. Default `"header"`.
- `onError`: `(size, maxSize) => Response` to build your own `413` response.

The full list is in `ecosystem/hooks/body-size-limiter/README.md`.

## Header mode and stream mode

- `"header"` reads the `Content-Length` header. A body without it (a chunked body) gets `411 Length Required`.
- `"stream"` measures the body itself. Use it if your platform or proxy sends bodies without `Content-Length`.

```ts title="src/hooks.ts"
export const onRequest = [bodySizeLimiter({ mode: "stream" })];
```

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/jwt-auth'
---

# JWT Auth Plugin

This plugin reads a JSON Web Token from the `Authorization: Bearer` header and checks its signature. The token payload is put on `ctx.user`.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add jwt-auth
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add jwt-auth --force`.

## Register

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { jwtAuth } from "../ecosystem/plugins/jwt-auth/jwt-auth";

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(jwtAuth({ secret: process.env.JWT_SECRET }));
};
```

The secret must be at least 32 bytes. Make one with `openssl rand -base64 32`.

## Options

- `secret`: key for HMAC algorithms (HS256, HS384, HS512).
- `publicKey`: key for RS and ES algorithms.
- `algorithm`: default `"HS256"`.
- `issuer`, `audience`: claims the token must have.
- `requireExpiration`: reject tokens without `exp`. Default `true`.

The full list is in `ecosystem/plugins/jwt-auth/README.md`.

## Protect routes

Once registered, every route needs a valid token. Open a route with `auth: false` in its `config.ts`. Require a role with `roles`:

```ts title="api/health/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };
```

```ts title="api/admin/config.ts"
export default { auth: { required: true, roles: ["admin"] } };
```

- A missing or bad token gets `401`. A missing role gets `403`.
- The token is checked before validation, so `401` comes before `422`.
- A method export overrides the route default: `export const POST = { auth: true };`.
- WebSocket routes follow the same `config.ts` rule.

To type the `auth` key in `config.ts`, add this to `src/types.ts`:

```ts title="src/types.ts"
declare module "burger-api" {
  interface RouteConfig {
    auth?: boolean | { required?: boolean; roles?: string[] };
  }
}
```

## Sign tokens

Use `signJwt` in a login route. Set `expiresIn` (seconds), because tokens without `exp` are rejected.

```ts title="api/login/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";
import { signJwt } from "../../../ecosystem/plugins/jwt-auth/jwt-auth";

export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  // Check the credentials first, then sign.
  const token = await signJwt(
    { sub: "user-123", roles: ["admin"] },
    { secret: process.env.JWT_SECRET!, expiresIn: 3600 }
  );
  return Response.json({ token });
}
```

```ts title="api/login/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };
```

## Use it in a handler

```ts title="api/me/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ userId: ctx.user?.sub });
}
```

## Related

- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)
- [OIDC](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/oidc)
- [Authentication Example](https://burger-api.com/docs/examples/authentication)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/api-key-auth'

# API Key Auth Plugin

This plugin reads an API key from a request header and checks it. A valid key is put on `ctx.apiKey`.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add api-key
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add api-key --force`.

## Register

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { apiKey } from "../ecosystem/plugins/api-key/api-key";

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(apiKey({ keys: [process.env.API_KEY!] }));
};
```

## Options

- `keys`: list of valid keys.
- `validate`: async function to check a key yourself, for example against a database.
- `header`: header to read. Default `"X-API-Key"`.

The full list is in `ecosystem/plugins/api-key/README.md`.

## Protect routes

Once registered, every route needs a valid key. Open a route with `auth: false` in its `config.ts`:

```ts title="api/health/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };
```

Change one method only with a method export:

```ts title="api/items/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };      // GET stays public
export const POST = { auth: true };  // POST needs a key
```

A missing or wrong key gets `401`. The key is checked before validation, so a bad key gets `401` even when the body is invalid. WebSocket routes follow the same `config.ts` rule.

## Use it in a handler

```ts title="api/private/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ apiKey: ctx.apiKey });
}
```

## Related

- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)
- [JWT Auth](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/jwt-auth)
- [Authentication Example](https://burger-api.com/docs/examples/authentication)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/basic-auth'
---

# Basic Auth Plugin

This plugin checks HTTP Basic credentials (username and password in the `Authorization` header). It calls your `validate` function and puts the returned user on `ctx.user`. Use it for internal tools and admin panels.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add basic-auth
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add basic-auth --force`.

## Register

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { basicAuth } from "../ecosystem/plugins/basic-auth/basic-auth";

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(
    basicAuth({
      validate: async (username, password) => {
        const user = await db.users.findByUsername(username);
        if (user && (await Bun.password.verify(password, user.passwordHash))) {
          return { id: user.id, username: user.username, roles: user.roles };
        }
        return null;
      },
    })
  );
};
```

`validate` must return a user (`id`, `username`, optional `roles`) or `null`.

## Options

- `validate`: `(username, password) => Promise<user | null>`. Required.
- `realm`: name shown in the browser login prompt. Default `"Restricted"`.

The full list is in `ecosystem/plugins/basic-auth/README.md`.

## Protect routes

Once registered, every route needs credentials. Open a route with `auth: false` in its `config.ts`. Require a role with `roles`:

```ts title="api/health/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };
```

```ts title="api/admin/config.ts"
export default { auth: { required: true, roles: ["admin"] } };
```

- Bad or missing credentials get `401`, and the browser shows its login prompt.
- A user without a listed role gets `403`.
- Credentials are checked before validation, so `401` comes before `422`.

## Use it in a handler

```ts title="api/me/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ id: ctx.user?.id, username: ctx.user?.username });
}
```

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [JWT Auth](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/jwt-auth)
- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/session'
---

# Session Plugin

This plugin keeps per-visitor data behind a cookie and exposes it as `ctx.session`. Use it for login state, carts or preferences.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add session
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add session --force`.

## Register

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { session } from "../ecosystem/plugins/session/session";

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(session({ secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET }));
};
```

Always set `secret` in production. It signs the session ID.

## Options

- `secret`: key that signs session IDs.
- `cookie`: cookie name. Default `"session_id"`.
- `maxAge`: session lifetime in seconds. Default `86400` (24 hours).
- `store`: where sessions are kept. Default is in memory, which is lost on restart. Use a shared store in production.

The full list, including the store interface, is in `ecosystem/plugins/session/README.md`.

## Protect routes

By default every route needs a session. The check runs before validation, so `401` comes before `422`. Open routes, such as login, with `auth: false` in `config.ts`:

```ts title="api/login/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };
```

## Log in and log out

Write to `ctx.session` to save data and set the cookie. Set it to `undefined` to end the session.

```ts title="api/login/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const { username } = await ctx.json();
  // ...check the credentials...
  ctx.session = { userId: "42", username };
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}
```

```ts title="api/logout/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  ctx.session = undefined;
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}
```

## Good to know

- Having a session does not mean the user logged in. Check a field your login sets, such as `ctx.session?.userId`.
- Sessions have no roles. A route that lists `auth.roles` always gets `403`. Check roles yourself in a route `transform` hook instead.

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [JWT Auth](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/jwt-auth)
- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/oidc'
---

# OIDC Plugin

This plugin checks tokens from an OpenID Connect provider, such as Google, Auth0 or Entra ID. It verifies the token with the provider's public keys and puts the claims on `ctx.user`.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add oidc
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add oidc --force`.

## Register

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { oidc } from "../ecosystem/plugins/oidc/oidc";

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(
    oidc({
      issuer: "https://accounts.google.com",
      audience: "my-client-id",
    })
  );
};
```

## Options

- `issuer`: provider URL. Required. Must match the token `iss` exactly.
- `audience`: when set, the token `aud` must contain it.
- `algorithms`: allowed algorithms. Default `["RS256", "ES256"]`. Only these two are supported.

The full list is in `ecosystem/plugins/oidc/README.md`.

## Protect routes

Once registered, every route needs a valid token. Open a route with `auth: false` in its `config.ts`. Require a role with `roles` (read from the token's `roles` claim):

```ts title="api/public/config.ts"
export default { auth: false };
```

```ts title="api/admin/config.ts"
export default { auth: { required: true, roles: ["admin"] } };
```

- A missing or bad token gets `401`. A missing role gets `403`.
- The token is checked before validation, so `401` comes before `422`.
- If the provider cannot be reached, the request gets `503`. The client can retry.

## Use it in a handler

```ts title="api/me/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  return Response.json({ sub: ctx.user?.sub, email: ctx.user?.email });
}
```

All token claims are on `ctx.user`.

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [JWT Auth](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/jwt-auth)
- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/env'
---

# Env Plugin

This plugin checks your environment variables when the app starts. It checks types, fills in defaults, and stops startup with a clear list of problems. It is not an auth plugin and adds no request hooks.

## Install

```bash
burger-api add env
```

To update the copy later, run `burger-api add env --force`.

## Register

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { env } from "../ecosystem/plugins/env/env";

export default (burger: PluginRegistrar) => {
  burger.usePlugin(
    env({
      required: {
        DATABASE_URL: { type: "url" },
        JWT_SECRET: { type: "string", validate: (value) => value.length >= 32 },
      },
      optional: {
        PORT: { type: "number", default: 3000 },
      },
    })
  );
};
```

With this config, a missing `DATABASE_URL` or a `PORT` of `"abc"` stops startup.

## Options

- `required`: variables that must be set.
- `optional`: variables that may be missing, usually with a `default`.

Each variable takes:

- `type`: `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"url"` or `"json"`.
- `default`: value used when the variable is missing or empty.
- `validate`: `(value) => boolean` for extra checks.

The full list is in `ecosystem/plugins/env/README.md`.

## Use the values

Read them from `process.env` as usual. Defaults are written back as strings, so `PORT` is `"3000"`. Parse numbers and booleans where you use them.

## Related

- [Hooks & Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration)
- [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/ai-assistance/agent-skills'
---

# AI Agent Skills

An Agent Skill is a set of markdown files that teaches your AI coding assistant how BurgerAPI works. Install it once. Your assistant finds it on its own and uses it when you ask about routes, hooks, validation, or the CLI.

Skills follow the [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io) open standard.

## Install

### New project

`burger-api create` asks:

```text
◇  Add AI agent skills? (recommended for agentic IDEs)
│  Yes / No
```

Answer Yes (the default). Every new project also gets an `AGENTS.md` file with project rules for AI agents.

### Existing project

```bash
burger-api skills install
```

To see what is available and what is installed:

```bash
burger-api skills available
burger-api skills list
```

## Where the files go

The skill is written to two folders with the same content:

```text
.agents/skills/burger-api/     # read by OpenCode, Codex, and other agentskills.io tools
.claude/skills/burger-api/     # read by Claude Code
```

If your tool reads a different folder, copy the skill there. The files are plain markdown.

## Related

- [Skills CLI Command Reference](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/skills)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/installation'
---

# CLI Installation

Install the Burger API CLI to create projects, add hooks and plugins, and build for production.

```bash
bun add -g @burger-api/cli
```

Or use it without installing:

```bash
bunx @burger-api/cli create my-project
```

For standalone executables and manual Bun setup, see [Installation](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/installation).

# Create Command

`burger-api create <project-name>` creates a new project and installs its dependencies. It asks a few questions: whether you want API routes, pages or WebSocket routes, their folders and prefixes, and whether to add AI agent skills.

```bash
burger-api create my-api
```

Then:

```bash
cd my-api
bun run dev
```

## Options

- `--lang ts|js`: TypeScript (default) or JavaScript.
- `--yes` (or `--defaults`): skip the questions and use the defaults.
- `--pages`: add a `src/pages/` folder for web pages.
- `--ws`: add WebSocket routes.
- `--no-api`: no API routes (use with `--pages` or `--ws`).
- `--api-dir <dir>`, `--api-prefix <prefix>`: change where API routes live and their URL prefix.
- `--no-skills`: do not add AI agent skills.

```bash
burger-api create my-api --lang js
burger-api create my-app --pages --ws
```

## What you get

Every project gets `src/index.ts`, an `src/api/` folder with an example route, `burger.build.ts` with your build settings, and `AGENTS.md` with project rules for AI coding agents. See [CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli#project-structure) for the full layout.

## Related

- [Add Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/add)
- [Dev Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/dev)
- [Burger API CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/generate'
---

# Generate Command

`burger-api generate <type> <name>` (alias `g`) scaffolds route directories, WebSocket route directories, and local hook/plugin stubs. Run it from your project root.

It follows your project language: pass `--lang js`, or the CLI detects a JavaScript project from `jsconfig.json`. Otherwise it generates `.ts` files.

## `burger-api generate route <path>`

Creates a route directory under the configured `apiDir` (default `src/api`) with convention files: `route`, `schema`, `openapi`, `hooks`, and `config`.

**Options:**

- `-l, --lang <lang>`: `ts` or `js` (detected from `jsconfig.json`)
- `--no-schema`: skip `schema.ts`
- `--no-openapi`: skip `openapi.ts`
- `--no-hooks`: skip `hooks.ts`
- `--no-config`: skip `config.ts`

```bash
burger-api generate route users
burger-api generate route products/[id]
burger-api generate route files/[...]
burger-api generate route users --no-hooks --no-config
```

## `burger-api generate ws <path>`

Creates a WebSocket handler directory under the configured `wsDir` (default `src/websocket`) with `ws`, `hooks`, and `config` convention files.

**Options:**

- `-l, --lang <lang>`: `ts` or `js` (detected from `jsconfig.json`)
- `--no-hooks`: skip `hooks.ts`
- `--no-config`: skip `config.ts`

```bash
burger-api generate ws chat
burger-api generate ws notifications/[room]
```

## `burger-api generate hook <name>`

Creates a local hook factory in `ecosystem/hooks/<name>/`.

**Options:**

- `-l, --lang <lang>`: `ts` or `js` (detected from `jsconfig.json`)
- `--local`: read the ecosystem catalog from the local checkout instead of GitHub. See [Local mode](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli#local-mode).

```bash
burger-api generate hook rate-limit
```

If a working implementation with that name already exists in the official ecosystem, the CLI prints a warning suggesting `burger-api add <name>` instead. The local stub is still created.

## `burger-api generate plugin <name>`

Creates a local plugin in `ecosystem/plugins/<name>/`.

**Options:**

- `-l, --lang <lang>`: `ts` or `js` (detected from `jsconfig.json`)
- `--local`: read the ecosystem catalog from the local checkout instead of GitHub. See [Local mode](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli#local-mode).

```bash
burger-api generate plugin audit-log
```

The same ecosystem warning as `generate hook` applies.

# Add Command

`burger-api add <name...>` copies official hooks and plugins into your project. Hooks go to `ecosystem/hooks/`, plugins to `ecosystem/plugins/`. After copying, the CLI prints the code to register them in `src/hooks.ts` or `src/plugins.ts`.

```bash
burger-api add cors
burger-api add cors logger rate-limiter
burger-api add jwt-auth
```

See what is available with `burger-api list`, or browse the [Ecosystem](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/introduction).

## Updating a copy

The files are yours to read and edit, so updating the CLI does not change them. To replace a copy with the latest version, add `--force`:

```bash
burger-api add cors --force
```

`--force` overwrites the copy, so re-apply any edits you made. `burger-api doctor` tells you which copies are out of date. See [Doctor Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/doctor).

## Related

- [List Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/list)
- [Generate Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/generate): create your own hook or plugin
- [Burger API CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/list'
---

# List Command

`burger-api list` (alias `ls`) shows the official hooks and plugins with a short description of each. Install one with `burger-api add <name>`.

```bash
burger-api list
```

The list comes from GitHub and is saved for a few hours. If GitHub is not reachable, the CLI shows the saved list and says so.

# Skills Command

`burger-api skills` adds AI agent skills to your project. A skill is a set of markdown files that teaches AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and others) how BurgerAPI works, so they write code that fits your project.

```bash
burger-api skills install            # the burger-api skill
burger-api skills list               # skills in this project
burger-api skills available          # skills you can install
```

`skills install` puts the files in `.agents/skills/<name>/` and `.claude/skills/<name>/`. Agents find them there on their own. If your tool reads skills from another folder, copy the files there.

To update an installed skill, add `--force`:

```bash
burger-api skills install burger-api --force
```

`burger-api create` offers to install the `burger-api` skill for you.

## Related

- [Create Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/create)
- [Burger API CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/dev'
---

# Dev Command

`burger-api dev` runs your app while you develop. When you save a file in `src/`, `ecosystem/` or `burger.build.ts`, it restarts the app. New projects run it with `bun run dev`.

```bash
burger-api dev
burger-api dev --port 3000
```

Options:

- `-p, --port <port>`: the port (default `$PORT`, else `4000`).
- `-f, --file <file>`: the entry file (default `src/index.ts`).

`dev` turns on debug output, so errors show stack traces and response validation problems in detail. If the app crashes, `dev` keeps running and starts it again when you save a fix.

For production, use `burger-api build`. See [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build).

## Related

- [Create Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/create)
- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [Burger API CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build'
---

# Build Command

`burger-api build` builds your app for production. It finds your routes at build time, so the deployed app does not need your source folders.

```bash
burger-api build
```

The entry defaults to `src/index.ts` (or `.js`/`.mjs`). Pass another file as the first argument if yours is elsewhere.

## Targets

Choose where the app will run with `--target`:

| Target | Output | Run or deploy it with |
|---|---|---|
| `bun` (default) | `.build/bundle/app.js` | `burger-api start` |
| `node` | `.build/bundle/app.js` | `node .build/bundle/app.js` |
| `cloudflare` | `.build/cloudflare/index.ts` | `wrangler dev` / `wrangler deploy` |
| `deno` | `.build/deno/index.ts` | `deno serve .build/deno/index.ts` |
| `vercel` | `api/index.ts` | `vercel dev` / `vercel --prod` |

```bash
burger-api build                        # Bun
burger-api build --target=node          # Node: run "bun add @burger-api/node-server" first
burger-api build --target=cloudflare    # also creates wrangler.toml if you have none
```

For Cloudflare, Deno and Vercel, the build also creates the platform's config file (`wrangler.toml`, `deno.json` or `vercel.json`) when you do not have one. It never overwrites yours.

If your app has pages, the Bun and Node builds put the page files next to `app.js`. Deploy the whole `.build/bundle/` folder.

See the [Deployment](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun) guides for each platform, and [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility) for what each target supports.

## Bun-only code

When you build for Node, Cloudflare, Deno or Vercel, the CLI warns about files that use Bun-only APIs (`Bun.*`, `bun:*` imports, or WebSocket publish), because they will fail on that platform. Remove that code before you deploy. A WebSocket route on Vercel fails the build, because Vercel does not support WebSockets.

## Options

- `--target <platform>`: `bun` (default), `node`, `cloudflare`, `deno` or `vercel`.
- `--outfile <path>`: where to write the build.
- `--minify`: minify the output (Bun and Node).
- `--sourcemap <type>`: `inline`, `linked` or `none` (Bun and Node).
- `--compile`: build a standalone executable instead. See [Build Exec](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build-exec).
- `--no-bun-check`: skip the Bun-only code warning.

## Related

- [Build Exec](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build-exec)
- [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility)
- [Burger API CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build-exec'
---

# Build Exec Command (build:exec)

`burger-api build:exec` builds your app into a single executable file. It runs on a machine without Bun installed. Your routes, pages and files are inside it.

```bash
burger-api build:exec
```

The file is written to `.build/executable/`. To build for another operating system, pass `--target`:

```bash
burger-api build:exec --target bun-linux-x64
burger-api build:exec --target bun-windows-x64
burger-api build:exec --target bun-darwin-arm64
```

Options:

- `--outfile <path>`: where to write the executable. On Windows, `.exe` is added if missing.
- `--target <target>`: the operating system and CPU to build for.
- `--no-minify`: build without minifying the code.
- `--no-bytecode`: build without bytecode (the app starts more slowly).

`burger-api build --compile` does the same thing.

## Related

- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [Burger API CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/inspect'

# Inspect Command

`burger-api inspect` shows what the CLI finds in your project: your settings, API routes with their methods, pages, WebSocket routes, hooks and plugins. Run it from your project root.

```bash
burger-api inspect
```

Use it to check a project after adding routes. If a route is missing from the list, check its folder name and that it is inside your API folder (`src/api` by default).

## `--json`

```bash
burger-api inspect --json
```

Prints the same information as one JSON object, for scripts and AI agents.

## Related

- [Doctor Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/doctor)
- [Burger API CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/doctor'
---

# Doctor Command

`burger-api doctor` checks your project for common problems. Run it from your project root when something does not work, or in CI.

```bash
burger-api doctor
```

It checks that:

- Bun is 1.4.4 or newer, and Node (if installed) is new enough for the `node` build target.
- `burger-api` is installed.
- Your entry file (`src/index.ts`), `tsconfig.json` and `burger.build.ts` exist and load.
- Every route file loads without errors.
- Hooks and plugins you added with `burger-api add` are up to date.

Each problem comes with what to do about it. Doctor exits `0` when every check passes and `1` when one fails, so you can run it in CI next to `bun run typecheck`.

## Out-of-date hooks and plugins

`burger-api add` copies hooks and plugins into your project, so updating the CLI does not update them. Doctor tells you when a copy is out of date and prints the command to refresh it:

```bash
burger-api add jwt-auth --force
```

An auth plugin (`jwt-auth`, `api-key`, `basic-auth`, `session`, `oidc`) that misses a security fix makes doctor fail. Other out-of-date copies are warnings. Hooks and plugins you wrote yourself are not checked.

`--force` overwrites the copy, so re-apply any edits you made to it.

## `--json`

```bash
burger-api doctor --json
```

Prints the results as one JSON object (`{ version, ok, errorCount, checks: [{ name, pass, message }] }`) for scripts and CI. The exit code is the same.

## Related

- [Inspect Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/inspect)
- [Create Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/create)
- [CLI Installation](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/installation)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility'
---

# Runtimes & Compatibility

You write your app once and run it on Bun in development. To deploy, run `burger-api build --target=<platform>` for one of five targets: Bun, Node.js, Cloudflare Workers, Deno, or Vercel.

Version requirements:

- **Bun 1.4.4 or newer** for the framework and CLI.
- **Node 24.22.1+ or 26.12.1+** for Node.js deployments.

## Feature matrix

| Feature | Bun | Node.js | Cloudflare Workers | Deno | Vercel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| File-based routing (`route.*`, `schema.*`, `hooks.*`, `openapi.*`, `config.*`) | Full | Full | Full | Full | Full |
| Hook lifecycle (all 6 points) | Full | Full | Full | Full | Full |
| Validation (`ctx.validated`, 422 + RFC 9457) | Full | Full | Full | Full | Full |
| OpenAPI + docs UI | Full | Full | Full | Full | Full |
| Providers (`ctx.services`) / Plugins | Full | Full | Full | Full | Full |
| `burger-api build --target` | `bun` (default) | `node` | `cloudflare` | `deno` | `vercel` |
| Long-running process | Yes | Yes | No (per-request) | Usually (Deploy: no) | No (per-invocation) |
| Filesystem at request time | Yes | Yes | No | Yes (Deploy: no) | No |
| Static assets | Yes | Yes | Yes (platform assets recommended) | Yes | Yes (platform assets recommended) |
| WebSocket | Yes | Yes (with `@burger-api/node-server`) | Yes | Yes | **No** |
| Pub/sub (`ws.publish`, `ctx.publish`) | Yes | No | No | No | No |
| `--compile` (standalone binary) | Yes | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A |

## WebSocket

WebSocket works on every target except Vercel. Vercel has no long-lived connections, so `burger-api build --target=vercel` fails if your project has WebSocket routes.

Pub/sub is Bun-only. See [WebSocket](https://burger-api.com/docs/websocket/overview) for a pattern that works everywhere, and [WebSocket on Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/websocket/overview#nodejs) for Node setup.

## Static assets

Production builds include your asset files, so they work on every target. On Cloudflare Workers and Vercel, use the platform's own static hosting (Cloudflare Assets, Vercel `public/`) for anything more than a few small files.

## Cloudflare Workers, Deno, and Vercel

- `burger-api build` finds your routes at build time. Your app does not read the filesystem at request time.
- Do not import `bun` in your app code. These runtimes cannot load it.
- The build gives you an entry file. You bundle and deploy it with the platform's own tool (`wrangler`, `deno`, `vercel`).

## Related

- [Deploy on Bun](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun)
- [Deploy on Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node)
- [Deploy on Cloudflare Workers](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/cloudflare)
- [Deploy on Deno](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/deno)
- [Deploy on Vercel](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/vercel)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun'
---

# Deploy on Bun

Bun is BurgerAPI's main runtime (Bun 1.4.4 or newer). Every feature works on Bun, including pages and WebSocket pub/sub.

You build your app with `burger-api build` and run the build with `burger-api start`.

## Entry file

```ts
// src/index.ts
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const app = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
});

// Read PORT so the host platform can assign one; fall back to 4000 locally.
const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 4000;
app.serve(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server running on http://localhost:${port}`);
});
```

The generated `package.json` maps the CLI commands to Bun scripts:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "burger-api dev",
    "start": "burger-api start",
    "build": "burger-api build src/index.ts",
    "typecheck": "bun check"
  }
}
```

## Local development

```bash
bun run dev
```

## Production build

```bash
bun run build   # AOT route scan + production bundle
bun run start   # serve the production build
```

## HTTPS

Most apps get HTTPS from what sits in front of them: a load balancer, a CDN such as Cloudflare, or a proxy such as nginx or Caddy. It handles the certificate and HTTP/2, and your app serves plain HTTP behind it. Your hosting platform usually sets this up for you. For WebSocket routes, the proxy must forward upgrade requests.

To serve HTTPS from the app itself, pass a certificate and key with the `tls` option:

```ts
// src/index.ts
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const app = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
  tls: process.env.TLS_CERT
    ? {
        cert: Bun.file(process.env.TLS_CERT),
        key: Bun.file(process.env.TLS_KEY!),
      }
    : undefined,
});

const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 4000;
app.serve(port);
```

- Set `TLS_CERT` and `TLS_KEY` to the full paths of your PEM files. Use full paths: the production build runs from its own folder, so relative paths do not work.
- Without the variables, the app serves plain HTTP. That keeps local development simple.
- WebSocket routes use `wss://` when `tls` is set.
- `tls` works with `serve()` on Bun. On Node, Cloudflare Workers, Deno and Vercel, the platform handles HTTPS and the option is ignored.

## VPS or Docker

Build and run the production bundle, then expose the port:

```dockerfile
FROM oven/bun
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN bun install
RUN bun run build
EXPOSE 4000
CMD ["bun", "run", "start"]
```

`@burger-api/cli` is a devDependency, so run a plain `bun install` (not a production-only install) before `bun run build` and `bun run start`; both scripts invoke the CLI. Alternatively, skip the CLI at runtime by starting the bundle directly with `CMD ["bun", ".build/bundle/app.js"]`, which works from a production-only install.

## Related

- [Quick Start](https://burger-api.com/docs/quick-start)
- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [Deploy on Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node)
- [Deploy on Cloudflare Workers](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/cloudflare)
- [Deploy on Vercel](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/vercel)
- [Deploy on Deno](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/deno)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node'
---

# Deploy on Node.js

BurgerAPI runs on Node.js 24 and newer with the `@burger-api/node-server` package.

## Build and run

```bash
bun add @burger-api/node-server
burger-api build --target=node
node .build/bundle/app.js
```

The build contains your routes, so the server does not need your `src/` folder. Copy `.build/bundle/` to your server and run it with Node. The port comes from `$PORT` (default `4000`).

WebSocket routes work too. `ws.subscribe()`, `ws.publish()` and `ctx.publish()` are Bun-only: on Node, keep your own list of connections. See [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility).

## Without the CLI

If you define routes in code instead of files, start the server yourself with `serve()`:

```ts title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

export const burger = new Burger({
  apiRoutes: [
    {
      path: "/api/hello",
      handlers: {
        GET: () => Response.json({ message: "Hello from Node.js!" }),
      },
    },
  ],
});
```

```ts title="src/server.ts"
import { serve } from "@burger-api/node-server";
import { burger } from "./index.ts";

const server = serve(burger, { port: 3000 });
server.on("listening", () => {
  console.log("Server running on http://localhost:3000");
});
```

```bash
node src/server.ts
```

Node runs TypeScript files directly. Write the `.ts` extension in relative imports (`./index.ts`), as above.

## Related

- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [WebSocket on Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/websocket/overview#nodejs)
- [Deploy on Bun](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/cloudflare'

# Deploy on Cloudflare Workers

Your BurgerAPI app runs on Cloudflare Workers without code changes. The CLI builds it, and Cloudflare's `wrangler` tool runs and deploys it.

## Build and deploy

```bash
burger-api build --target=cloudflare
npx wrangler dev        # run it locally
npx wrangler deploy     # deploy it
```

The build writes `.build/cloudflare/index.ts`. If you do not have a `wrangler.toml` yet, it also creates one:

```toml title="wrangler.toml"
name = "my-api"
main = ".build/cloudflare/index.ts"
compatibility_date = "2025-06-01"
compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"]
```

Run the build again after you change your code.

## What works on Workers

API routes, hooks, plugins, validation, OpenAPI and WebSocket routes all work. Pages from `src/pages/` and WebSocket pub/sub (`ws.publish()`, `ctx.publish()`) are Bun-only. Code that uses `Bun.*` does not run on Workers; the build warns you about it. See [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility).

## Without the CLI

If you define routes in code instead of files, export a fetch handler yourself:

```ts title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger, toFetchHandler } from "burger-api";

const burger = new Burger({
  apiRoutes: [
    {
      path: "/api/hello",
      handlers: {
        GET: () => Response.json({ message: "Hello from Cloudflare Workers!" }),
      },
    },
  ],
});

export default { fetch: toFetchHandler(burger) };
```

Then set `main = "src/index.ts"` in `wrangler.toml`.

## Related

- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [Deploy on Bun](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun)
- [Deploy on Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/vercel'
---

# Deploy on Vercel

Your BurgerAPI app runs as a Vercel Function without code changes. The CLI builds it, and the `vercel` tool runs and deploys it.

## Build and deploy

```bash
burger-api build --target=vercel
npx vercel dev       # run it locally
npx vercel --prod    # deploy it
```

The build writes `api/index.ts`, the place Vercel looks for functions. If you do not have a `vercel.json` yet, it also creates one that sends every request to your app:

```json title="vercel.json"
{
  "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/api" }]
}
```

Run the build again after you change your code.

## What works on Vercel

API routes, hooks, plugins, validation and OpenAPI work. WebSocket routes do not: Vercel Functions cannot keep a connection open, so the build fails if your app has any. Pages from `src/pages/` and code that uses `Bun.*` are Bun-only. See [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility).

## Without the CLI

If you define routes in code instead of files, write `api/index.ts` yourself:

```ts title="api/index.ts"
import { Burger, toFetchHandler } from "burger-api";

const burger = new Burger({
  apiRoutes: [
    {
      path: "/api/hello",
      handlers: {
        GET: () => Response.json({ message: "Hello from Vercel!" }),
      },
    },
  ],
});

export const runtime = "nodejs";

export default { fetch: toFetchHandler(burger) };
```

Add the `vercel.json` above so every path reaches it.

## Related

- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [Deploy on Bun](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun)
- [Deploy on Cloudflare Workers](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/cloudflare)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/deno'

# Deploy on Deno

:::warning Deno is in maintenance mode
In October 2026 the Deno team [joined Cloudflare](https://deno.com/blog/cloudflare).
The Deno runtime gets bug-fix and security releases for about one year, and
Deno Deploy shuts down about six months after the announcement. BurgerAPI keeps
the Deno target working, but for new hosted projects we recommend
[Cloudflare Workers](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/cloudflare).
:::

Your BurgerAPI app runs on Deno without code changes. The CLI builds it, and `deno serve` runs it.

## Build and run

```bash
burger-api build --target=deno
deno serve --port 8000 .build/deno/index.ts
```

The build writes `.build/deno/index.ts`. If you do not have a `deno.json` yet, it also creates one that tells Deno where to find `burger-api`. Run `deno serve` on your own server or in a container.

Run the build again after you change your code.

## What works on Deno

API routes, hooks, plugins, validation, OpenAPI and WebSocket routes work. Pages from `src/pages/`, WebSocket pub/sub and code that uses `Bun.*` are Bun-only. See [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility).

## Without the CLI

If you define routes in code instead of files, export a fetch handler yourself:

```ts title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger, toFetchHandler } from "burger-api";

const burger = new Burger({
  apiRoutes: [
    {
      path: "/api/hello",
      handlers: {
        GET: () => Response.json({ message: "Hello from Deno!" }),
      },
    },
  ],
});

export default { fetch: toFetchHandler(burger) };
```

```json title="deno.json"
{
  "imports": {
    "burger-api": "npm:burger-api@^1.0.0-beta",
    "burger-api/": "npm:burger-api@^1.0.0-beta/"
  }
}
```

```bash
deno serve --port 8000 src/index.ts
```

## Related

- [Build Command](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build)
- [Deploy on Cloudflare Workers](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/cloudflare)
- [Deploy on Bun](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/performance/overview'
---

# Performance

BurgerAPI does most of its work once, when the app starts. Each request then does only what it needs. You do not need to configure anything to get this.

## What this means for your code

- **Write routes the normal way.** Static, `[param]`, and wildcard routes are all fast to match.
- **Read only what you use.** `ctx.query` and other context fields are parsed when you first read them. A handler that never reads the query never parses it.
- **Set response changes on `ctx.set`.** Status, headers, and cookies are applied once at the end. If you set nothing, your `Response` is returned as is.
- **Hooks cost little.** Each route's hooks are prepared at startup, not looked up on every request.

For measured results, see [burger-api-benchmarks](https://github.com/isfhan/burger-api-benchmarks).

## Related

- [Request Context](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/request-handling)
- [Benchmarks](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/benchmarks)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core/burger-class'
---

# Burger Class

`Burger` is your app. Create it in `src/index.ts` and call `serve()` to start it.

```ts title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const app = new Burger({
  apiDir: "./src/api",
});

await app.serve(4000);
```

The constructor takes [Server Options](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/server-options). Hooks, plugins, providers and OpenAPI metadata live in their own files, not here. See [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration).

## App files

| File | Role |
|------|------|
| `src/index.ts` | `new Burger({...})` and `serve()` only |
| `src/hooks.ts` | Global hooks |
| `src/plugins.ts` | Register plugins with `usePlugin` |
| `src/providers.ts` | Register services with `provide` |
| `src/openapi.config.ts` | OpenAPI metadata and docs UI |
| `burger.build.ts` | Build settings, read by the CLI only |

## Methods

### serve(port?, callback?)

Starts the server on Bun.

```ts
await app.serve(4000, () => {
  console.log("Server running at http://localhost:4000");
});
```

- `port`: default `4000`.
- `callback`: runs once the server has started.

See [Deployment](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun).

### usePlugin(plugin)

Registers a plugin. Call it in `src/plugins.ts`, which default-exports a function:

```ts title="src/plugins.ts"
import type { PluginRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { apiKey } from "../ecosystem/plugins/api-key/api-key";

export default function (burger: PluginRegistrar) {
  burger.usePlugin(apiKey({ keys: ["demo-api-key-123"] }));
}
```

Registering the same plugin twice has no extra effect. See [Hooks and Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins) and [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration#plugins-and-providers).

### provide(name, service)

Registers a service. It is created once and shared as `ctx.services.<name>`. Call it in `src/providers.ts`:

```ts title="src/providers.ts"
import type { ProviderRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { createDb } from "./db";

export default function (burger: ProviderRegistrar) {
  burger.provide("db", createDb());
}
```

See [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers) and [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration#plugins-and-providers).

### websocket(path, handlers)

Adds a WebSocket route in code:

```ts
app.websocket("/chat", {
  open(ws) {
    ws.send("connected");
  },
  message(ws, message) {
    ws.send(message);
  },
});
```

Routes added this way work in dev only. `burger-api build` does not include them. For production, add a file under `src/websocket/`. See [WebSocket](https://burger-api.com/docs/websocket/overview).

### fetchHandler()

Builds a standard fetch handler `(request) => Promise<Response>`. It is async, so `await` it. Use it with `Bun.serve`, `Deno.serve`, Vercel, Cloudflare Workers or Node 24+. Some page features work only with `serve()` on Bun. See [Compatibility](https://burger-api.com/docs/compatibility).

### toFetchHandler(app)

A function, not a method. It wraps the app as a fetch handler you can export directly:

```ts
import { Burger, toFetchHandler } from "burger-api";

const app = new Burger({ apiRoutes });

// Cloudflare Workers / Vercel
export default { fetch: toFetchHandler(app) };

// Deno
Deno.serve(toFetchHandler(app));
```

These runtimes have no filesystem, so pass the `apiRoutes` from `burger-api build`. See [Deployment](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun).

### createNodeWsBridge(options)

Low-level WebSocket support for Node. You rarely need it. Use `serve(app)` from [`@burger-api/node-server`](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node) instead: it starts HTTP and WebSocket for you.

```ts
import { serve } from "@burger-api/node-server";
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const app = new Burger({ apiRoutes, wsRoutes });

serve(app, { port: 3000 });
```

See [WebSocket](https://burger-api.com/docs/websocket/overview#nodejs).

### getServer()

Returns the server object. Useful in tests to stop the server:

```ts
const server = app.getServer();
if (server?.isRunning()) server.stop();
```

## Related

- [Server Options](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/server-options)
- [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration)
- [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/core/server-options'
---

# Server Options

`new Burger({...})` takes a `ServerOptions` object. All options are optional. Most apps set none or only a few.

```ts title="src/index.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

const burger = new Burger({
  apiPrefix: "v1",
  debug: true,
});

burger.serve(4000);
```

## Options

| Option | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `apiDir` | `string` | Folder with API routes. Default `./src/api`. |
| `pageDir` | `string` | Folder with pages. Default `./src/pages` if it exists. |
| `wsDir` | `string` | Folder with WebSocket routes. Default `./src/websocket` if it exists. |
| `apiPrefix` | `string` | URL prefix for API routes. Default `'api'`. Use `''` to mount at `/`. |
| `pagePrefix` | `string` | URL prefix for pages. Default `''`. |
| `debug` | `boolean` | Show stack traces and response validation details. On by default when `NODE_ENV=development` (`burger-api dev` sets it). `false` turns it off. |
| `validation` | object | `coerce`, `responseValidation` (`'off' \| 'dev' \| 'enforce'`), `errorFormat` (`'plain' \| 'problem+json'`), `status`, `errorRenderer`. See [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration). |
| `openapi` | `OpenAPIConfig` | OpenAPI settings for apps without `src/openapi.config.ts`. See [OpenAPI](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/openapi). |
| `title`, `description`, `version` | `string` | Fallback OpenAPI metadata. Prefer `src/openapi.config.ts`. |
| `hostname` | `string` | Hostname for `serve()` to bind. |
| `maxRequestBodySize` | `number` | Largest request body in bytes for `serve()`. Bigger bodies get `413`. Bun's default is 128 MB. |
| `tls` | object | `cert` and `key` (plus optional `passphrase`, `ca`, `serverName`). `serve()` then speaks HTTPS. Bun only. See [HTTPS](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun#https). |

## Set by the build

`burger-api build` fills these in for you. You do not set them by hand in a normal project.

| Option | What the build puts there |
|--------|-------------|
| `apiRoutes`, `pageRoutes`, `wsRoutes` | Routes found at build time. They replace `apiDir`, `pageDir`, `wsDir`. |
| `assetRoutes` | Files from `<pageDir>/assets/`. |
| `globalHooks`, `pluginsModule`, `providersModule` | Your `src/hooks.ts`, `src/plugins.ts` and `src/providers.ts`. |
| `runtimeTarget` | The `--target` platform. |

In dev, BurgerAPI reads your folders and app files directly. See [CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli).

## Advanced

`jit`, `engine` and `adapter` are for tests and special runtimes. Leave them at their defaults.

## Types

Import `ServerOptions` from `burger-api` if you build the options object separately. TypeScript flags a typo such as `apiDri`. Run `bun run typecheck` to check.

## Related

- [Burger Class](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/burger-class)
- [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration)
- [CLI Tool](https://burger-api.com/docs/getting-started/cli)
- [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/api/context-set'
---

# ContextSet

`ContextSet` is the type of `ctx.set`. Use it to change the response status and headers. For usage, see [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation).

```ts
interface ContextSet {
  status?: number;
  headers?: Record<string, string | string[]> | Headers;
}
```

## Fields

| Field | Type | What it does |
|-------|------|--------------|
| `status` | `number` | Sets the response status. It does not replace an error status (400 or higher). |
| `headers` | `Record<string, string \| string[]> \| Headers` | Adds headers to the response. Your values win. An array value adds every entry. `set-cookie` values are added, not replaced. |

`ctx.set.headers` always exists, so you can assign to it directly.

```ts
ctx.set.headers = { "x-request-id": ctx.headers.get("x-request-id") ?? "none" };
```

## Related

- [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation)
- [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/api/validation-types'
---

# Validation Types

Type reference for validation. For how validation works, see [Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/validation).

## Per-method schema

`schema.ts` exports one object per HTTP method. Each slot is optional and takes a Zod or [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev/) schema.

```ts title="src/api/products/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = { query: z.object({ limit: z.coerce.number().optional() }) };
export const POST = {
  body: z.object({ name: z.string().min(1) }),
  response: { 200: z.object({ id: z.string() }) },
};
```

| Slot | Checks |
|------|--------|
| `params` | Path parameters |
| `query` | Query string |
| `headers` | Request headers |
| `cookies` | Cookies |
| `body` | JSON body |
| `response` | Handler output, keyed by status (`200`) or class (`2xx`) |

## ctx.validated

Valid data lands on `ctx.validated.params`, `.query`, `.headers`, `.cookies` and `.body`. A key exists only if its slot has a schema. Wrap the handler with `defineRoute` to type it:

```ts title="src/api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  return Response.json({ limit: ctx.validated.query.limit });
});
```

## ValidationError

A failed check throws `ValidationError` (status 422). It has the failing `slot` and a list of issues:

```ts
interface ValidationIssue {
  path: (string | number)[];
  message: string;
  code?: string;
}
```

If no `onError` hook handles it, the client gets an RFC 9457 Problem Details response. See [Validation Errors](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/errors).

## Options

`new Burger({ validation: { ... } })` takes `coerce`, `responseValidation` and `errorFormat`. See [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration).

## Related

- [Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/validation)
- [Schema Definition](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/schema)
- [Validation Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/configuration)
- [Server Options](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/server-options)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/api/hook-types'
---

# Hook Types

Type reference for hooks. All types come from `burger-api`. For how hooks work, see [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system).

## ForwardHook and ResponseHook

```ts
type ForwardHookResult =
  | Response
  | ((response: Response) => Response | Promise<Response>)
  | void
  | undefined;

type ResponseHookResult = ForwardHookResult;

type ForwardHook = (
  ctx: BurgerContext
) => ForwardHookResult | Promise<ForwardHookResult>;

type ResponseHook = (
  ctx: BurgerContext
) => ResponseHookResult | Promise<ResponseHookResult>;

type Hook = ForwardHook | ResponseHook;
```

`ForwardHook` is used by `onRequest` and `beforeRoute`. `ResponseHook` is used by `afterRoute` and `mapResponse`. Each slot takes one hook or an array. See [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types) for what each return value does.

## ErrorHook

```ts
type ErrorHook = (
  error: Error,
  ctx: BurgerContext
) => Response | void | undefined | Promise<Response | void | undefined>;
```

Return a `Response` to handle the error. Return `undefined` to let the next `onError` hook try. If no hook handles it, BurgerAPI sends a default error response.

## RouteHooks

```ts
interface RouteHooks {
  transform?: TransformMap;
  beforeRoute?: ForwardHook | ForwardHook[];
  afterRoute?: ResponseHook | ResponseHook[];
  mapResponse?: ResponseHook | ResponseHook[];
  onError?: ErrorHook | ErrorHook[];
}
```

The shape of a route `hooks.ts`. It has no `onRequest`.

## GlobalHooks

```ts
interface GlobalHooks extends RouteHooks {
  onRequest?: ForwardHook | ForwardHook[];
}
```

The shape of `src/hooks.ts` and of a plugin's `hooks`.

## TransformMap

```ts
type TransformMap = Record<string, (ctx: BurgerContext) => unknown>;
```

Each key is a field to add to `ctx`. Each function returns that field's value. See [Global Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global#transform).

## Related

- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)
- [Hook Return Types](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/return-types)
- [Key Concepts](https://burger-api.com/docs/key-concepts)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api'
---

# Request API

Every handler and hook gets `ctx`, a `BurgerContext`. This page lists what you can read from it.

Examples assume `import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";`.

## Quick reference

| Property | What it is |
|----------|------------|
| `ctx.params` | Path parameters from `[param]` folders |
| `ctx.wildcardParams` | Segments matched by a `[...]` folder |
| `ctx.query` | Query string values. See [Query Parsing](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/query-parsing) |
| `ctx.cookies` | Cookies, by name |
| `ctx.headers`, `ctx.method`, `ctx.url` | The usual request fields |
| `ctx.json()`, `ctx.text()`, `ctx.arrayBuffer()` | Read the body |
| `ctx.body` | The raw body stream |
| `ctx.request` | The original `Request` |
| `ctx.validated` | Data that passed your schemas |
| `ctx.route` | The matched route. See [Route Metadata](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/route-metadata) |
| `ctx.config` | The route's `config.ts` values, read-only |
| `ctx.services` | Services from `src/providers.ts` |
| `ctx.ip` | The client address |
| `ctx.set` | Status, headers and cookies for the response. See [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation) |

## Params and query

```ts title="src/api/users/[id]/route.ts"
export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const { id } = ctx.params;
  const { limit = "10" } = ctx.query;
  return Response.json({ id, limit });
}
```

## Body

```ts
export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const body = await ctx.json<{ name: string }>();
  return Response.json({ name: body.name });
}
```

You can call `ctx.json()` more than once. If the route has a `body` schema, read `ctx.validated.body` instead. It is typed and already checked.

## ctx.validated

Add a `schema.ts` and wrap the handler with `defineRoute`. `ctx.validated` is then typed from the schema.

```ts title="src/api/products/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = { query: z.object({ limit: z.coerce.number().optional() }) };
```

```ts title="src/api/products/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  const { limit } = ctx.validated.query; // number | undefined
  return Response.json({ limit });
});
```

See [Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/validation).

## ctx.services

Shared services such as a database client. They are the same for every request and read-only. For per-request values, use a [transform](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/global#transform) hook. See [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers).

## ctx.ip

The client address from the socket. It never comes from headers like `X-Forwarded-For`. It is set on Bun `serve()` and on [`@burger-api/node-server`](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node). With `toFetchHandler` it is `undefined`.

## Related

- [Request Context](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/request-handling)
- [Response Mutation](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation)
- [Burger Class](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/burger-class)
- [Key Concepts](https://burger-api.com/docs/key-concepts)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/api/response-mutation'

# Response Mutation

Handlers return a standard `Response`. To change the status, headers or cookies from a hook or a handler, use `ctx.set`. BurgerAPI applies it to the response at the end of the request.

```ts title="src/api/users/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function POST(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  ctx.set.status = 201;
  ctx.set.headers = {
    "x-total": "42",
    "set-cookie": "session=abc; HttpOnly; Path=/",
  };
  return Response.json({ created: true });
}
```

What you get:

- `ctx.set.status` changes the status of a success response. An error status (400 or higher) stays as it is.
- `ctx.set.headers` adds headers. Your values win over the response's own headers.
- An array value adds every entry. `set-cookie` is always added, so cookies from the handler and from `ctx.set` both reach the client.
- A `ctx.set` from `onRequest` also applies to 404s, errors, pages and `/docs`.

To change the response body or read the response, use an [after hook](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/after) instead.

## Related

- [ContextSet](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/context-set)
- [After Hooks](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/after)
- [Hook System](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system)

---
url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/api/route-metadata'
---

# Route Metadata

`ctx.route` tells you which route handled the request.

```ts
interface RouteMeta {
  path: string;    // the requested path, e.g. "/api/users/123"
  pattern: string; // the route pattern, e.g. "/api/users/:id"
}
```

`pattern` includes the API prefix. For a static route, `path` and `pattern` are the same.

```ts title="src/api/products/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  console.log(`served by ${ctx.route?.pattern}`); // "/api/products"
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}
```

The type is `RouteMeta | undefined`, so use `?.`. In a matched handler it is always set.

Use it for logs, metrics keyed by route, or building links.

## Related

- [File-Based Routing](https://burger-api.com/docs/routing/file-based-routing)
- [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/api/query-parsing'
---

# Query Parsing

Read the query string with `ctx.query`. It is an object of `string | string[]`.

```ts title="src/api/posts/route.ts"
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";

// GET /api/posts?tag=bun&tag=ts&page=2
export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const { tag, page } = ctx.query; // tag: ["bun", "ts"], page: "2"
  return Response.json({ tag, page });
}
```

- A key that repeats becomes an array, in order.
- `+` becomes a space, like `URLSearchParams`.
- Bad percent-encoding is kept as is. It never throws.
- Values are always strings. To get numbers or booleans, add a query schema. See [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query).

You do not need `new URL(ctx.url).searchParams`. Use `ctx.query`.

## Related

- [Request API](https://burger-api.com/docs/api/request-api)
- [Query Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/query)

url: 'https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/testing'

# Testing

Test routes without a server. Build the app, get its fetch handler, and send it real `Request` objects. It runs the same routes and hooks as the server.

Use `bun test`. Put tests in `test/` and name them `*.test.ts`.

## Build the app in the test

Do not import `src/index.ts` in a test: it starts the server. Build the app in a helper instead:

```ts title="test/helpers.ts"
import { Burger } from "burger-api";

export async function createHandler() {
  const app = new Burger({ apiDir: "./src/api", apiPrefix: "/api" });
  return app.fetchHandler();
}
```

Run `bun test` from the project root, so `./src/api` resolves.

## Test a route

```ts title="test/notes.test.ts"
import { expect, test } from "bun:test";
import { createHandler } from "./helpers";

const handler = await createHandler();

test("GET /api/hello returns JSON", async () => {
  const res = await handler(new Request("http://localhost/api/hello"));

  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
  expect(await res.json()).toEqual({ message: "Hello, world!" });
});

test("POST /api/notes rejects an empty name with 422", async () => {
  const res = await handler(
    new Request("http://localhost/api/notes", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ name: "" }),
    })
  );

  expect(res.status).toBe(422);
});
```

These tests assume a `hello` route and a `notes` route with a `body` schema. The URL needs a host, but only the method and path matter.

## Test with a plugin or a fake service

For a focused test, pass the routes yourself with `apiRoutes`. Then the app does not scan files. Add plugins with `pluginsModule` and fake services with `providersModule`:

```ts title="test/secret.test.ts"
import { expect, test } from "bun:test";
import { Burger } from "burger-api";
import type { PluginRegistrar, ProviderRegistrar } from "burger-api";
import { apiKey } from "../ecosystem/plugins/api-key/api-key";
import { GET } from "../src/api/users/route";

const app = new Burger({
  apiRoutes: [{ path: "/api/users", handlers: { GET } }],
  pluginsModule: {
    default: (burger: PluginRegistrar) =>
      burger.usePlugin(apiKey({ keys: ["test-key"] })),
  },
  providersModule: {
    default: (burger: ProviderRegistrar) =>
      burger.provide("db", { listUsers: async () => [{ id: 99, name: "Test User" }] }),
  },
});

const handler = await app.fetchHandler();

test("rejects a request without a key", async () => {
  const res = await handler(new Request("http://localhost/api/users"));
  expect(res.status).toBe(401);
});

test("reads users from the fake db", async () => {
  const res = await handler(
    new Request("http://localhost/api/users", { headers: { "X-API-Key": "test-key" } })
  );
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
});
```

If the route validates input, add its `schema` to the `apiRoutes` entry too.

If a test fails with an unexpected status, log `await res.text()` to see the error.

## Related

- [Providers](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/providers)
- [Validation](https://burger-api.com/docs/core-concepts/validation)
- [Hooks and Plugins](https://burger-api.com/docs/ecosystem/hooks-plugins)
- [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration)

# Error Handling Patterns

- **Validation errors:** a failed request gets `422` with an RFC 9457 problem details body. See [Validation Error Handling](https://burger-api.com/docs/validation/errors).
- **Unknown routes:** get `404` with a problem details body.
- **Throw an error:** throw `NotFoundError`, `UnauthorizedError`, `ForbiddenError` or another `HTTPError`. BurgerAPI turns it into the right response. Add an `onError` hook to change how errors look.
- **Stop in a hook:** return a `Response` (for example a `429` or `503`) from `onRequest` or `beforeRoute` to stop the request. For auth, throw `UnauthorizedError` from `transform` instead. See [Auth goes in transform](https://burger-api.com/docs/hooks/system#auth-goes-in-transform).
- **Return from a handler:** `return Response.json({ error: "Not found" }, { status: 404 });`.
- **Debug details:** stack traces appear only when debug is on (`debug: true`, or `NODE_ENV=development`, which `burger-api dev` sets). See [Configuration](https://burger-api.com/docs/core/configuration).

```ts title="src/api/products/[id]/route.ts"
import { NotFoundError } from "burger-api";
import type { BurgerContext } from "burger-api";
import { products } from "../store";

export async function GET(ctx: BurgerContext) {
  const product = products.find((p) => p.id === ctx.params.id);
  if (!product) throw new NotFoundError("Product not found");
  return Response.json(product);
}
```

- [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety)
- [Deployment](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/deployment)

# TypeScript Types

TypeScript checks your code before it runs. BurgerAPI gives you types for requests, schemas, hooks and plugins.

Check your project with:

```bash
bun run typecheck
```

## Type a handler from its schema

Wrap the handler with `defineRoute(schema, handler)`. Pass the export from `schema.ts`, and `ctx.validated` gets its types:

```ts title="api/search/schema.ts"
import { z } from "zod";

export const GET = { query: z.object({ q: z.string().optional() }) };
```

```ts title="api/search/route.ts"
import { defineRoute } from "burger-api";
import { GET as GetSchema } from "./schema";

export const GET = defineRoute(GetSchema, (ctx) => {
  ctx.validated.query; // { q?: string }
  return Response.json(ctx.validated.query);
});
```

You can also write the type by hand: `ctx: BurgerContext<typeof GetSchema>`. A route without a schema uses plain `BurgerContext`.

Route hooks that read `ctx.validated` use `defineHooks(schema, hooks)` the same way.

## Types for convention files

| File | Type |
|------|------|
| route `schema.ts` | `export const GET = {...} satisfies MethodSchema;` |
| route `openapi.ts` | `export const GET = {...} satisfies OpenAPIMeta;` |
| route `hooks.ts` | `RouteHooks` |
| route `config.ts` | `RouteConfig` |
| `src/hooks.ts` | `GlobalHooks` |
| `src/plugins.ts` | `PluginRegistrar`, `Plugin` |
| `src/providers.ts` | `ProviderRegistrar` |
| `openapi.config.ts` | `satisfies OpenAPIConfig` |
| `burger.build.ts` | `satisfies Partial<BuildConfig>` |

JavaScript projects get the same checks through JSDoc, for example `/** @type {Partial<import('burger-api').BuildConfig>} */`.

## Add your own types

Some types start empty, and you fill them in. Put this in `src/types.ts` (`burger-api create` makes this file for you):

```ts title="src/types.ts"
import type { Database, User } from "./my-types";

declare module "burger-api" {
  // ctx.services, from burger.provide()
  interface BurgerServices {
    db: Database;
  }

  // values you set in transform hooks
  interface BurgerContext {
    tenant: string;
  }

  // ctx.user and ws.user (auth plugins add their fields here too)
  interface BurgerAuthUser {
    userId?: string;
  }

  // your own config.ts keys
  interface RouteConfig {
    auth?: boolean | { required?: boolean; roles?: string[] };
  }
}
```

## What is not typed

- `ctx.params` is always `Record<string, string>`. Add a `params` schema and use `ctx.validated.params` for typed values.
- `ctx.wildcardParams` is always `string[]`.
- `ctx.json()` returns `any`. Use `ctx.json<T>()` to give it a type.

# Benchmarks

All BurgerAPI benchmarks live in one place: the [burger-api-benchmarks](https://github.com/isfhan/burger-api-benchmarks) repository.

It has the test setup, the method, and the reports. Follow its README to run the benchmarks on your own machine.

# Deployment

Build your app with `burger-api build`, then run it on your target. Each target has its own guide:

- [Bun](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/bun): `burger-api build`, then `burger-api start`.
- [Node.js](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/node): `serve(app)` from `@burger-api/node-server`.
- [Cloudflare Workers](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/cloudflare)
- [Vercel](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/vercel)
- [Deno](https://burger-api.com/docs/deployment/deno)

Edge targets use `toFetchHandler(app)`. See [CLI Build](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build) and [Build Exec](https://burger-api.com/docs/cli/build-exec).

- [Error Handling Patterns](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/error-handling)
- [Type Safety](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/type-safety)
- [Benchmarks](https://burger-api.com/docs/advanced/benchmarks)
